papers.title: When Retrieval Is Not Enough: Obsolete Facts in Agent Memory
papers.abstract: Memory-agent benchmarks often collapse retrieval and answer generation into one score, making it hard to tell whether a failure comes from missing an update or from not using an update that was already retrieved. We examine this distinction on the single-hop FactConsolidation task of MemoryAgentBench. With Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct on 6K-history BM25 accuracy drops from 45% to 32% when the retrieved evidence budget grows from 64 to 512 tokens, even though a gold-assisted post-hoc audit finds the newest statement in every retrieved set. Most of the errors occur on questions that also contain an obsolete statement version. Under a frozen prompt and equal four-statement evidence size, replacing one unrelated statement with the obsolete competing statement reduces accuracy from 100% to 44.6% for Qwen2.5 and from 100% to 87.8% for Qwen3-14B, with all 50 harmful paired flips classified as stale. A 32K-history replication likewise favors BM25-64 over BM25-512 (69% versus 58%). These results suggest that retrieving the correct fact is not enough. An obsolete competing statement can be more harmful than an unrelated piece of evidence of the same size.

We study this question using the MemoryAgentBench’s FactConsolidation task (Hu et al., 2026). For example, the memory may first state that the author of The Marriage of Figaro is Pierre Beaumarchais and later state that it is Thomas Kyd. Under the benchmark’s chronology, Thomas Kyd is then the correct answer.

papers.title: RPSD: Retrieval-Privileged On-Policy Self-Distillation with Optimal Transport
papers.abstract: Sequential recommendation predicts a user's next interaction from historical behavior. Recent LLM-based methods recast this task as generative recommendation and increasingly adopt reinforcement learning such as GRPO for post-training. However, these methods suffer from two limitations, namely credit-blind optimization, where a sequence-level reward is shared across all generated tokens, and collaborative-blind supervision, where each training signal is derived from a single user and ignores behavioral patterns shared across similar users. To address both issues, we propose Retrieval-Privileged on-policy Self-Distillation (RPSD). For credit-blind optimization, we introduce on-policy self-distillation (OPSD), in which a teacher with privileged knowledge re-evaluates the student's on-policy response, and the token-level confidence difference between the student and teacher reshapes the shared sequence-level advantage into token-specific credit. However, the privileged knowledge in vanilla OPSD is still derived from a single user, leaving collaborative-blind supervision unresolved. We therefore ground the teacher in collaborative behavioral evidence from similar users. Specifically, we use temporally aware optimal transport (OT) to compare interaction trajectories across users by jointly considering item similarity and temporal structure, and further apply diversity-aware selection to retain complementary trajectories as privileged evidence. In this way, on-policy self-distillation provides fine-grained token-level credit, while OT enriches the teacher with structured cross-user evidence. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to bring on-policy self-distillation to sequential recommendation and to use cross-user behavior as its privileged signal. Extensive experiments across multiple real-world datasets demonstrate that RPSD achieves state-of-the-art performance.

papers.intro:
Sequential recommendation predicts the next item that a user will interact with from the ordered history of past interactions and it is central to content, e-commerce, and media platforms Ma et al. (2026) where user interests change over time (Hidasi et al., 2016; Kang and McAuley, 2018). Traditional methods treat the sequential recommendation problem as next-item prediction over an interaction sequence, evolving from recurrent and self-attention encoders (Hidasi et al., 2016; Kang and McAuley, 2018) to graph-based and contrastive variants, which model higher-order transitions and augment sparse signals (He et al., 2020; Xie et al., 2022; Qiu et al., 2022). Although these models are effective and efficient, they represent items as opaque identifier embeddings and reason over co-occurrence statistics rather than the semantics of what a user consumed, which limits generalization when histories are short. An ideal recommender, however, should do more than name which candidate comes next and it should ground that choice in why the recommended item matches the user’s evolving interest.

Although these models are effective and efficient, they represent items as opaque identifier embeddings and reason over co-occurrence statistics rather than the semantics of what a user consumed, which limits generalization when histories are short. An ideal recommender, however, should do more than name which candidate comes next and it should ground that choice in why the recommended item matches the user’s evolving interest.

Large language models (LLMs) address the semantic side of this gap by casting recommendation as language generation, either unifying recommendation tasks in a text-to-text format (Geng et al., 2022; Rajput et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2025a; Li et al., 2026; Kong et al., 2025b) or fine-tuning a pretrained LLM to reason over item titles and name the next item directly in text (Bao et al., 2023; Liao et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025). To align such an LLM with the recommendation objective, reinforcement learning has become a standard post-training recipe. Recent work adapts GRPO (Shao et al., 2024) to LLM-based recommendation, tailoring its reward and credit assignment to the ranking structure of the task. For example, Rank-GRPO (Zhu et al., 2026) moves the reward from the whole sequence to each individual rank, so that later positions in the list get their own credit instead of sharing one signal. RecZero (Kong et al., 2025a) keeps GRPO unchanged but reshapes the rollout into explicit analyze-user, analyze-item, match, and rate steps, replacing exact-match correctness with a reward graded by the predicted rating’s closeness to the true one. However, these adaptations only change which part of a response the reward is applied to. Rank-GRPO gives each rank its own reward and RecZero gives each reasoning step its own, but in both cases a single number is still shared by all the tokens inside that rank or step. The source of the reward is left untouched as well. Whether it is computed over the sequence, the rank, or the step, it always comes from the next item of the user being scored. A reward of this kind can confirm that a recommendation is right, but one user’s interactions are a thin basis for learning why, since a short history reflects accident as much as preference. The same pattern observed across many users with comparable histories is far more dependable, and it is the only evidence available when a single history is too short to be read on its own. Therefore, two problems remain unaddressed, namely credit-blind optimization and collaborative-blind supervision.

Credit-blind optimization concerns how the reward is assigned. Not every token in a response contributes equally to the recommendation. Most tokens provide shared linguistic or formatting structure, while only a small subset determines which item is ultimately selected. GRPO nevertheless assigns the same sequence-level advantage to every generated token, providing no indication of which tokens actually make the recommendation correct. On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) (Zhao et al., 2026) provides a promising direction for addressing this limitation. By deriving token-level guidance from a more informed teacher on the same on-policy response, OPSD enables finer-grained credit assignment while preserving the original policy and inference procedure. These properties make it particularly appealing for sequential recommendation. However, the effectiveness of OPSD is ultimately limited by the informativeness of the teacher’s privileged knowledge. If the teacher lacks sufficient behavioral context, the resulting token-level guidance may still be inadequate for capturing the preference signals underlying the target item. Vanilla OPSD typically relies on the ground-truth label as the privileged signal, which tells the model which candidate is correct but provides limited information about why that candidate matches the user’s preference. Therefore, the second issue collaborative-blind supervision is introduced. Existing generative recommenders derive supervision from the user alone, overlooking regularities shared across similar users.

papers.title: M4Bench: Evaluating Procedural Specification for Clinical EHR Derivation Agents
papers.abstract: Clinical research over electronic health records depends on derived variables whose definitions sit outside the schema, in item codes, time windows, missingness rules, and output-grain choices that change cohorts and downstream conclusions. We introduce M4Bench, 28 clinical derivation tasks across 15 task families on MIMIC-IV and eICU, to test whether AI coding agents can reproduce such derivations and how clinician-reviewed agent skills change their results. Its controls decompose the value of skills into specification completeness, delivery format, and schema familiarity. In a Docker-isolated Codex campaign (GPT 5.4 Mini and GPT 5.5), skills raise reward by 0.136 over the no-skill baseline, with 26 of 28 tasks improving. Specification completeness accounts for most of this gain: on an eight-task control subset, an operational spec alone raises reward by 0.162, and skills add only 0.024 on top, indistinguishable from zero. On a ten-task subset, decoy skills score like no skill and raw reference SQL nearly matches targeted skills, arguing against generic context or the skill format as the explanation. Schema obfuscation and restructuring preserve 86% and 70% of the skill gain (GPT 5.4 Mini, 26 MIMIC-IV tasks), a descriptive robustness check rather than a bound on memorization. A descriptive Claude Code replication on all 28 tasks (Opus 4.7 and Sonnet 4.6, 560 runs) is directionally consistent (+0.120, 21 of 28 tasks improving). These gains are partial agreement with the reference, not completed tasks: only 25 of 280 with-skill and 13 of 280 no-skill Codex runs pass every strict check, and skills barely change which rows agents return (key F1 +0.003). Skills are released as a versioned, clinician-reviewable markdown delivery format, with a family-level reference-validity audit. M4Bench releases tasks, skills, evaluation code, and sanitized per-run evidence as an open-source benchmark.

papers.intro:
Observational clinical research using electronic health records (EHRs) commonly relies on derived variables: severity scores such as Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) (Vincent et al., 1996) and Acute Physiology Score III (APS-III) (Knaus et al., 1991), organ-dysfunction measures such as Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO) acute kidney injury staging (KDIGO Acute Kidney Injury Work Group, 2012) and Model for End-Stage Liver Disease (MELD) (Kamath et al., 2001), and cohort-defining phenotypes such as suspected infection and Sepsis-3 (Singer et al., 2016). These variables are rarely available as simple columns. They are reconstructed from raw tables whose clinical meaning is distributed across item identifiers, units, documentation practices, time windows, and dataset-specific conventions, and the implementation choices behind a single derivation change cohort membership, score distributions, and downstream conclusions in observational studies (Johnson et al., 2017; Johnson et al., 2018; Ostropolets et al., 2023).

A SOFA implementation, for example, needs the score definition plus how vasopressors are encoded, how oxygenation variables are paired, how ventilation status changes respiratory scoring, and how missing components are handled in a specific database release. This procedural knowledge is held by clinicians and embedded in community concept code such as the MIT-LCP MIMIC-Code repository (Johnson et al., 2018), but no benchmark we are aware of represents it as an auditable agent artifact.

Rather than asking whether an agent can answer clinical questions in free text, M4Bench asks whether a coding agent can reproduce declared EHR research derivations and whether explicit procedural specifications change that behavior. papers.title: A Heart Means Recursion: Exploring Visual Meaning and Communication in VLMs
papers.abstract: Do vision-language models (VLMs) share our ability to communicate visually? We share preliminary findings, starting from a surprising observation: simple visual symbols like a red heart can strongly influence model behavior on seemingly unrelated tasks, such as steering models towards recursive solutions on simple coding problems. Notably, this steering effect is largely implicit, as models' direct interpretations and thinking traces about visual symbols diverge substantially from their observed behavior. In visual communication between models, this leads to a generation--interpretation gap: while models tend to send shape primitives that they (and humans) find intuitive, these visual cues often fail to steer other models. In further communication games involving abstract concepts and stories, models can creatively use visuals to transmit meaning to one another, although some communications remain non-intuitive to humans. These findings reveal that VLMs might be capable of rich, creative, and visually-grounded communication, but their interpretation and production of visual meaning diverges from human conventions in surprising ways. Together this work highlights both the promise and challenges of visual communication between humans and VLMs.

papers.intro:
Humans have a long history of visual communication. We encode and transfer meaning through shapes, colors, and spatial arrangements (Fan et al., 2020; Hawkins et al., 2023; Garrod et al., 2007). Vision-language models (VLMs) are trained on billions of images reflecting our visual culture: photographs, diagrams, icons, charts, and art. Frontier VLMs now demonstrate impressive visual understanding, from solving complex multi-discipline problems involving visual inputs (Yue et al., 2024; Lu et al., 2024) to spatial reasoning over visual scenes (Chen et al., 2024). Yet reasoning about visual content is different from communicating through it. Do VLMs share our ability to communicate visually?

Vision-language models (VLMs) are trained on billions of images reflecting our visual culture: photographs, diagrams, icons, charts, and art. Frontier VLMs now demonstrate impressive visual understanding, from solving complex multi-discipline problems involving visual inputs (Yue et al., 2024; Lu et al., 2024) to spatial reasoning over visual scenes (Chen et al., 2024). Yet reasoning about visual content is different from communicating through it. Do VLMs share our ability to communicate visually?

We explore visual communication in VLMs, testing how deeply they absorb visual cues in their inputs and their ability to use visualizations to communicate ideas. We present three complementary investigations. First, we test whether simple visual symbols (shapes, colors, icons) systematically steer VLM behavior on non-visual tasks, and whether models can faithfully report these influences. Second, we study VLMs’ generation and interpretation of visualizations communicating abstract concepts and stories. Third, we evaluate alignment between model and human visual interpretation.

papers.title: Beyond the Readout: A Latent Numerical Frame Shared Across Modality and Operation
papers.abstract: When a multimodal model computes 17+35 from text or 91-39 from a rendered image, it produces the same answer, 52. Does it use one internal concept of number for both, or separate machinery for each path? Similarity metrics such as RSA or CKA cannot settle this question. They give the same score to identical and to rotated directions, and two representations can look alike only because both prepare the same output digits. We therefore use causal interventions. For four conditions (text or image, addition or subtraction), we learn a small subspace of Gemma4-12B-it's residual stream in which swapping coordinates swaps the model's answer. The subspaces answer three questions. First, do the conditions write numbers along the same directions? They do not. Reusing a subspace from text in an image on the same operation recovers only 53.2% of its causal effect. A single rotation and rescaling maps one subspace onto the other and raises recovery to 91.4%, so the conditions share one geometry expressed in different coordinates. Second, does this shared geometry only reflect the digit the model is about to print? To test this, we split each subspace into 9 directions that the output layer reads to choose the next digit and 13 directions that it cannot see. The 13 hidden directions still carry the number, yet changing them barely alters the digit being written. Third, what are these hidden directions for? A model must emit a multi-digit answer one digit at a time, so it can compute the full result early and keep it in reserve. When two numbers share their first digit, swapping the number in the hidden directions leaves the digit being written intact and redirects the next digit in 77.6% of cases. The model thus forms an abstract numerical concept upstream and unfolds it across time: multimodal representations share meaning through relational geometry across distinct coordinate frames.

When a multimodal language model computes an arithmetic result, it can reach the same number through fundamentally different inputs and operations. For example, the quantity 5252 can be reached by evaluating 17+3517+35 or 91−3991-39, presented as plain text or rendered as pixels in an image. Because all of these inputs arrive at the same mathematical truth, do they converge onto a shared internal representation of number?

For example, the quantity 5252 can be reached by evaluating 17+3517+35 or 91−3991-39, presented as plain text or rendered as pixels in an image. Because all of these inputs arrive at the same mathematical truth, do they converge onto a shared internal representation of number?

The Platonic Representation Hypothesis (Huh et al., 2024) suggests they should, positing that representations across diverse inputs converge toward a shared statistical model of reality. Yet when comparing different computational routes to the same number, “representational convergence” can mean three fundamentally distinct physical possibilities: Q1: Coordinate identity (shared directions). Does the network place numbers along the exact same linear directions regardless of input modality or operation? If so, an intervention discovered along one route will transfer directly to another without modification. Q2: Relational isomorphism (shared geometry in different coordinates). Do different routes preserve the same relative distances and displacements between numbers, but orient them along different coordinate axes? If so, direct transfer fails, but a rigid rotation and scaling can re-align them. Q3: Output interface artifact. Do representations for the same result under different conditions resemble each other only because the model is preparing to emit the exact same output token? If so, similarity reflects the shared digit vocabulary rather than an abstract concept of number.

Separating these hypotheses requires moving beyond passive similarity metrics. Representational Similarity Analysis (RSA) (Kriegeskorte et al., 2008), Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA) (Kornblith et al., 2019), and Canonical Correlation Analysis (CCA) (Hotelling, 1936) compare internal relationship structures and are invariant to orthogonal rotations by construction. Consequently, they yield identical scores under both Q1 and Q2, making them incapable of determining whether coordinates are shared or rotated. Furthermore, similarity metrics are inherently blind to Q3: any two tasks sharing an identical output vocabulary exhibit correlated late-layer representations simply from anticipating the output interface. Most fundamentally, representational agreement does not imply shared causal function (Usama and Chang, 2026) since models can exhibit matching geometry while using divergent causal mechanisms. By projecting out this readout interface, we can study the remaining latent numerical geometry in isolation (Q3).

papers.title: From Solver Trajectories to Teaching Trajectories: Cognition-Aligned Reasoning Distillation
papers.abstract: Knowledge distillation from large reasoning models (LRMs) often uses raw teacher trajectories as supervision. However, this practice creates a mismatch between the goal of distillation and the nature of teacher trajectories. Advanced LRMs typically improve their reasoning capabilities through reward-driven post-training, such as RLHF. This training optimizes them as strong solvers, rather than as teachers that produce reasoning processes smaller models can easily learn. Since smaller models have different "cognitive capacities" compared to their larger teachers, directly imitating raw teacher trajectories can sometimes be ineffective and often requires a substantial number of high-quality samples. To bridge this mismatch, we propose Cognition-Aligned Reasoning Distillation (CARD), an RL-based framework that transforms solver trajectories into teaching trajectories aligned with the student's cognition. Avoiding expensive resampling, our framework directly transforms existing trajectories. We optimize CARD with two reward signals: (1) a Distribution Alignment Reward that matches the student's predictive distribution, and (2) a Logical Coherence Reward that reduces misleading failed reasoning steps. Comprehensive evaluations across multiple student models and settings demonstrate that CARD outperforms distillation from raw teacher trajectories in in-domain settings while achieving substantial gains in out-of-distribution performance. Code is available at https://github.com/LiteSSLHub/CARD.

Existing reasoning distillation approaches typically fall into two broad categories, logits-based and trajectory-based. Logits-based methods Gu et al. (2024); Ko et al. (2024); Ko et al. These methods require access to the teacher’s output logits and further assume a shared vocabulary between teacher and student. Trajectory-based methods instead train the student directly on teacher-generated rationales via supervised fine-tuning (SFT) or its variants Gu et al. (2024); Ko et al. (2024); Li et al. (2025). 22 2 We use rationale to denote the CoT reasoning steps generated between a question and its final answer. As shown in Figure 2, this requires repeated teacher sampling and can be expensive for LRMs with large parameters. More critically, filtering only selects among existing teacher-generated trajectories and does not adapt them to the student. papers.title: AI-Assisted Discovery of CNOT Decompositions for Quantum Permutations on Constrained Topologies
papers.abstract: Efficient quantum circuit compilation is challenging for quantum computers, where limited qubit connectivity can introduce substantial overhead in the implementation of logical operations. Recent AI-assisted synthesis methods have shown considerable potential for reducing circuit complexity, but their role in uncovering principles that can guide the design of new deterministic compilation algorithms remains largely unexplored. In this work, we investigate this perspective for the synthesis of quantum permutations into CNOT circuits under constrained qubit connectivity. Using AlphaCNOT as an exploratory tool, we identify a recurring decomposition for remote transpositions that improves on the construction based on adjacent SWAP routing. For two qubits at graph distance $d>1$, the discovered pattern yields a topology-legal implementation using at most $6d-4$ CNOT gates, compared to the $6d-3$ gates required by the corresponding SWAP-based construction. We formalize this observation through a constructive proof to define Global Transpositions, a deterministic synthesis method that searches for a minimum-cost decomposition of an entire permutation into topology-aware logical transpositions. The resulting method subsumes optimal SWAP routing within its synthesis model and provides certified upper bounds on the topology-constrained CNOT cost. Our experiments also reveal circuits that cannot be expressed as concatenations of independently synthesized transpositions. Instead, these circuits exploit intermediate linear transformations that temporarily leave the permutation subgroup and combine partial effects of multiple logical operations, a mechanism we call intermediate CNOT fusion. Our results show that AI-assisted synthesis can support not only circuit optimization, but also the discovery of reusable identities, provable constructions, and hidden mechanisms in quantum circuit compilation.

papers.intro:
Limited qubit connectivity remains one of the main obstacles to the efficient execution of quantum circuits on current hardware. A quantum algorithm is typically designed in terms of logical qubits with no restrictions on which pairs may interact, whereas a physical quantum processor only permits two-qubit gates between adjacent vertices of a coupling graph Davis et al. (2020); Kissinger and Van De Griend (2020); Wu et al. (2023). Consequently, the practical cost of executing a quantum algorithm depends not only on its logical circuit, but also on how that circuit is compiled onto the target topology.

A standard approach to connectivity-constrained compilation is to insert SWAP gates whenever two logical qubits that must interact are not physically adjacent. Since a SWAP is commonly decomposed into three CNOT gates, minimizing the number of SWAPs provides a natural surrogate objective for reducing the two-qubit gate count. This approach is particularly relevant on current quantum devices, where two-qubit gates typically dominate both the execution error and the compilation overhead.

papers.title: Proactive Memory for Event-Driven LLM Agents
papers.abstract: Proactive LLM agents anticipate service opportunities from ongoing observations and accumulated history. Existing approaches emphasize recent context or retrieval of related memories, providing limited support for validating recurring behavioral regularities and assessing their applicability to the current event. We propose Proactive Memory (ProactMem), which organizes history into recent events, temporal trajectories, and behavioral regularities. Trajectory facts are checked against source events, and regularities are assessed through historical replay before being matched to current conditions. We also construct ProactiveStream, a longitudinal benchmark covering three application scopes, where agents process isolated event streams chronologically under episode-aware opportunity labels. On ProactiveStream, ProactMem achieves an overall effectiveness (F1) of 52.6%, a 21.4% relative improvement over the strongest of five external baselines. Code is available at: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/ProactMem-5351/.

papers.title: Enhancing Deep Learning Model Performance through Data Generation Strategies: Classification of Olive Tree Diseases
papers.abstract: Deep learning models are highly effective in a wide range of domains, particu larly in plant disease diagnosis. However, their performance is often limited by challenges such as insufficient data and class imbalance. In our work, we propose a comprehensive data generation strategy to overcome these limitations. First, we apply various data generation techniques, including traditional augmentation methods, CutMix, MixUp, and synthetic image generation using Deep Convolu tional Generative Adversarial Networks (DCGANs), to create new data samples. Second, we exploit this generated data in three scenarios: (S1) balancing class distribution in the original dataset, (S2) increasing the number of samples per class, and (S3) expanding the dataset while maintaining balanced classes. Third, we evaluate the impact of these data distributions (S1, S2, S3) on model perfor mance using the EfficientNetV2B0 architecture with pre-trained and fine-tuned weights. The experimental results show a substantial improvement in classifica tion accuracy, emphasizing the critical role of data diversity and class balance. These findings highlight the effectiveness and adaptability of the proposed strat egy of data generation and distribution for enhancing dataset quality, offering promising applications in plant disease detection and precision agriculture.

papers.title: SFE-O: An Ontology for Knowledge-Grounded AI in Supercritical CO$_2$ Biomass Extraction and Fractionation
papers.abstract: Supercritical CO$_2$ extraction (CO$_2$-SFE) offers a sustainable route for recovering high-value compounds from biomass while limiting the use of conventional organic solvents, but its design and interpretation require heterogeneous knowledge spanning biomass properties, operating conditions, mass transfer, and product fractionation, typically fragmented across technical reports, engineering models, external databases, and expert practice. This paper introduces SFE-O, a modular Web Ontology Language (OWL 2) ontology for supercritical CO$_2$ biomass extraction, structured around interconnected Biomass, Process, and Product dimensions and extended with explicit representations of process topology, parameter provenance, external and internal mass-transfer phenomena, and the Constant Extraction Rate (CER) / Falling Extraction Rate (FER) mechanisms. Computational dependencies among process quantities are represented explicitly, without embedding numerical solving in the ontology, so that input, measured, computed, externally retrieved, and fitted parameters remain traceable. SFE-O reuses established semantic resources (ChEBI, QUDT, OWL-Time, PROV-O) and is evaluated through a worked example that instantiates a real pilot-scale extraction batch, a reasoner-based consistency check, and a competency-question SPARQL query. The resulting knowledge model provides a machine-actionable foundation for querying, consistency checking, and mechanistic explanation of SFE processes, and establishes a knowledge layer that could support future ontology-grounded AI reasoning, a direction this paper motivates but does not evaluate.

papers.title: Ontology-guided multi-agent reasoning for explainable differential diagnosis
papers.abstract: Effective differential diagnosis depends on well structured and unambiguous patient case descriptions, since incomplete or ambiguous clinical information readily leads to diagnostic errors and inconsistent reasoning. Large Language Models (LLMs) have recently shown promising capabilities in medical question answering and clinical reasoning; however, even when achieving competitive performance on medical benchmarks, they often rely on pattern recognition learned from training data rather than grounded clinical evidence, and can generate plausible yet unsupported diagnostic conclusions. Their reasoning remains largely opaque, making it difficult for clinicians to assess the evidence and rationale behind a given recommendation. To address this gap, we propose an ontology-guided, multiagent differential diagnosis framework that replicates the iterative reasoning process of physicians. The framework grounds diagnostic inference in a structured, expert-curated medical knowledge base, enabling interpretation of symptoms, clinical findings, or disease relationships, while decomposing diagnosis into explicit, auditable reasoning steps. This ontology-based grounding constrains inference to evidence-backed associations, reducing hallucination and improving diagnostic transparency, traceability, and consistency. The system then identifies the most discriminative missing symptoms and generates targeted follow-up questions to reduce uncertainty through a process that mirrors to clinical inquiry. Together, these components improve the reliability, explainability, and diagnostic accuracy of AI-assisted differential diagnosis. The source code is publicly available.

papers.title: R\`enyi-Regularized Flow-Based Variational Inference for Bayesian Calibration
papers.abstract: Variational inference with normalizing flows provides a flexible posterior approximation for Bayesian model calibration, but struggles when the posterior has several modes separated by regions of low probability mass. We study this behavior in a two-parameter twin experiment and regularize the variational objective. Under Gaussian observation errors and a Gaussian prior, the corresponding minimization objective is the expected Tikhonov calibration objective minus the differential entropy of the approximating distribution. However, the expected Tikhonov term favors concentration near one of the modes, while entropy maximization does not guarantee multimodality. We introduce a regularization term based on R\'enyi divergence that encourages the approximate posterior to cover the prior support. In the connected bimodal case, a flow approximation represents both modes; in the case with well-separated modes, the flow and Gaussian mixture frequently miss one mode. The introduced regularization reduces the near-collapse fraction from 50% to 25%. While the regularization improves mode coverage in this experiment, it changes the Bayesian variational objective, introduces a trade-off in approximation accuracy, and does not provide a general solution to mode collapse.

papers.title: Learning to Formalize: Bridging Open-Ended Workloads and Fast Decision Models
papers.abstract: Decision models offer fast choices over sup- plied alternatives, while general-purpose large language models interpret open-ended tasks through flexible generation and reasoning at the cost of sequential decoding. Many work- loads expect a generative backend to determine what can be done and therefore provide no well-defined candidate list. We bridge this in- terface gap with a small candidate formalizer trained on offline teacher-generated lists. The formalizer constructs explicit, validated alter- natives from task context, and a frozen deci- sion model selects an entry. A motivating com- parison with official TypeSafe Jev-1.13.0 on 200 CALVIN-D test episodes reports 11% suc- cess with generic motions versus 46.5% with DeepSeek V4 Flash pose candidates. Sepa- rately, a six-arm privileged-state evaluation on 1,011 CALVIN-D validation annotations finds that a locally deployed decision model can achieve at most 52.6% task success rate with the fine-tuned formalizer, compared with 11.8% without it, and the end-to-end latency is kept to 2.09 s, whereas Qwen3.5-27B is 3.67 s with the exact experiment setting.

papers.intro:
Many workloads delegate an open-ended instruction to a backend language model and expect it to determine the next action. A tool-using assistant must infer an operation and its arguments; a workflow system must turn a request into an actionable next step; a robot must translate a goal into a control target. In these settings, the workload supplies context and an execution interface, while useful alternatives remain implicit or loosely described. The backend is expected to analyze the situation, construct alternatives, and return a decision.

Many workloads delegate an open-ended instruction to a backend language model and expect it to determine the next action. A tool-using assistant must infer an operation and its arguments; a workflow system must turn a request into an actionable next step; a robot must translate a goal into a control target. In these settings, the workload supplies context and an execution interface, while useful alternatives remain implicit or loosely described. The backend is expected to analyze the situation, construct alternatives, and return a decision.

General-purpose large language models (LLMs) are attractive backends because they can interpret open-ended requests and support multi-step reasoning (Brown et al., 2020; Wei et al., 2022). This flexibility has a latency cost: autoregressive decoding produces successive output tokens, and explicit intermediate reasoning can lengthen that sequence. Decision models offer a complementary interface. Their fast decision mode evaluates supplied alternatives and returns a typed choice without generating an extended answer (Almeida, 2026; AutoTrust AI Lab, 2026). However, this mode requires the application to specify what can be chosen. The schema defines admissible operations, but a useful candidate set must instantiate task-relevant operations and parameters for the current state. papers.title: The Trinity:Capability-Driven Recursive Self-Improvement for Multimodal Agents
papers.abstract: Multimodal intelligence can be viewed as human-guided co-evolution between worlds and agents through interaction. However, scaling this process faces two bottlenecks: constructing heterogeneous, verifiable environments is costly, and manual Harness iteration cannot keep pace with growing task diversity and complexity. A key insight is that tasks with different modalities and surface forms can share the same underlying capability requirements. We therefore introduce The Trinity, a recursive self-improvement framework coupling world generation with Harness evolution through three roles: Creator, Explorer, and Evolver. Drawing on verified execution trajectories, Evolver shifts the basis of task organization from surface categories to shared requirements, reorganizing the original task tree into a hierarchical capability tree. We introduce Capability-Driven Real2Sim2Real: for heterogeneous tasks at the same node, Creator abstracts their common requirements into simplified, verifiable simulated worlds for capability learning, while evaluation on original tasks measures transfer. Along this capability tree, Explorer progressively evolves reusable capability modules through selective inheritance, forming a Harness tree whose validated updates accumulate across iterations within a fixed topology. The resulting Harnesses specialize in different capabilities, motivating a Capability-Aware Harness Router that uses public task information to select compatible module configurations from the tree. Our evolved Harnesses improve mean performance by 34 points across 28 training benchmarks and 26 points across 18 unseen benchmarks, including two real-world embodied tasks.

papers.title: ATEMPO: Amortized Transfer Entropy Model Per-lag Over-Time
papers.abstract: When one time series informs another, the delay at which that information arrives determines if models can utilize this relationship effectively. A source may be strongly predictive at one delay but uninformative at neighboring lags. Therefore, fixed input windows may obscure this structure by bundling informative and irrelevant history together. Transfer entropy (TE) can recover these delays by measuring how much a source's past tells us about a target beyond the target's own history. However, existing TE estimators require separate fits across source and conditioning depths, with further estimation on local windows to track delays over time. We introduce ATEMPO, a diffusion-based transfer entropy estimator amortized over lags and time. ATEMPO samples source and conditioning depths during training and conditions explicitly on temporal position, allowing a single score network to estimate the full TE surface without refitting. Differencing this surface recovers when information arrives. Across synthetic datasets with ground-truth TE, ATEMPO achieves the lowest mean relative error among baselines, and on datasets with known lags, ATEMPO achieves $0.98\pm0.04$ lag-detection accuracy. ATEMPO requires a single fit across source depths $K=6$ and target depths $L=3$, whereas existing estimators require 18 separate fits to evaluate the same $K \times L$ grid. On three systems with time-varying lag, ATEMPO is the only estimator to maintain perfect lag-detection accuracy across all evaluated window lengths. These recovered delays improve downstream forecasting: ATEMPO-selected inputs reduce MSE on WEATHER-5K by 7.25%, while 120 selected inputs outperform the benchmark's 240-feature default by 4.6%. Across three brain-computer interface tasks, using ATEMPO-selected lags achieves the highest or equal-best $R^2$, improving mean $R^2$ by 4.1% relative to the strongest competing baseline.
papers.intro:
Multivariate time-series models must decide which variables and past observations to expose to the model. In practice, this is often handled by applying a fixed-width window uniformly to every variable, selecting its length and offset using a validation sweep (Nie et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2024; Han et al., 2026). Yet a variable may become informative only at a particular delay, the gap between when it is observed and when its influence arrives. If that delay is thirty steps, a window long enough to reach it also includes the twenty-nine intervening lags, most of which carry nothing. Although an ideal model could learn to ignore irrelevant history, with finite data these additional inputs increase estimation difficulty and can obscure the value of the delayed signal. This problem compounds in high-dimensional settings, where long common windows expose many potentially uninformative lags. Window selection therefore conflates two questions: whether a variable is informative and when its information arrives. Identifying the delay directly would allow a model to receive the informative observations without requiring all of the history in between. Transfer entropy (TE) (Schreiber, 2000) provides a natural way to identify such delays: it measures whether a source’s past provides information about a target beyond that already contained in the target’s own history.

papers.title: Noise Steering: Exploiting Wake Steering and Acoustic Directivity for Noise-Constrained Wind Farm Control via Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Existing noise mitigation strategies for wind farms usually consist in reducing turbines power output, without accounting for the wake interactions between them and the noise emission directivity. This leads to over-conservative policies and unexploited wind power. Yet, turbine yaw can simultaneously affect wake interactions and the direction of noise emission, offering an additional degree of freedom for farm-level noise control. We therefore propose Noise Steering, a model-free reinforcement learning (RL) strategy that jointly controls turbine yaw angles and power setpoints to maximise farm power while satisfying a local noise constraint in a defined region. To enable training at a reduced computational cost, a low-fidelity acoustic model is coupled with the steady-state FLORIS simulator. The RL agent effectively learns how to redirect wakes and noise directivity away from the protected region while redistributing power across the farm. On a six-turbine test farm, the policy satisfies the 40 dB noise constraint throughout the full range of turbulent winds, with an average power deficit of only 2% relative to greedy unimpeded control, and up to 7.7% at high wind speeds. In comparison, the industry-standard noise-reduced operation (NRO) baseline here generates an average power loss of 17%. When deployed in the higher-fidelity FAST.Farm simulator, the policy largely retains its performance under steady and turbulent inflow, despite differences in simulation fidelity. These results demonstrate the potential of combining yaw control and power derating through RL to improve the power-noise trade-off in wind farm operation.

Wind energy has become one of the fastest-growing sources of renewable electricity generation, with global installed capacity rising from 417 GW417\text{\,}\mathrm{GW} in 2015 to more than 1130 GW1130\text{\,}\mathrm{GW} by the end of 2024, which now accounts for about a quarter of all renewable power capacity worldwide [19]. Existing noise mitigation strategies mainly operate at the turbine level. Blade design optimisation [5, 23] and other approaches, such as blade trailing edge serrations [10], have been explored. On the turbine control side, industry standards define noise-reduced operation (NRO) modes for individual turbines [44], effectively limiting their rotational speed and power output. [14] provide an example of acoustic curtailment look-up table used to control the turbines. Model predictive control was used in [40] to find the optimal turbine controls (blade pitch and generator torque) to satisfy a noise level constraint. At the farm level, noise mitigation has mainly been addressed through layout optimisation [8, 48] and optimisation of individual NRO levels [39, 33, 42]. Moreover, Shah et al. [39] define uniform power derating of the turbines as a common control strategy by wind farm operators. These methods enable compliance with the noise regulation but reduce power generation of the wind farm, which leads to reduced revenue in real operation. The median loss in annual energy production (AEP) was estimated to be of 2.8% in France between 2020 and 2022 [46].

Meanwhile, an important share of wind farm control studies focuses on wake steering for power maximisation of the wind farm [4]. By misaligning turbines, yaw control redirects their wakes and can reduce velocity deficits for downstream turbines. Yaw control can also modify the spatial distribution (or directivity) of turbine noise. Wind turbine noise exhibits a dipole radiation pattern approximately aligned with the rotor axis (i.e., maximum with respect to the rotor normal) [34, 35], such that yawing a turbine changes the direction of maximum noise emission. The potential of exploiting noise directivity in wind farm operations has recently been highlighted by Shah et al. [39]. However, existing noise-reduction control strategies rely only on power adjustments and do not exploit turbine yaw control [14]. In this article, we extend the wake steering strategy, which targets power maximisation, to a novel farm-level noise-reduced operation strategy, referred to as Noise Steering. By controlling the yaw angles and NRO levels of the wind turbines, this control technique can maximise power generation while respecting a localised noise constraint.

papers.title: An Incremental Knowledge-Graph Learner Digital Twin for Evidence-Grounded Early Warning
papers.abstract: Early-warning models in learning analytics can identify learners at risk of failure or withdrawal, but the resulting alerts are often only weakly connected to inspectable learning evidence. A risk score may indicate that intervention is needed without showing which traces, assessment events, or temporal patterns justify the alert. This paper introduces an incremental Learner Digital Twin for evidence-grounded early warning, implemented as a lightweight knowledge graph. The twin is updated at temporal checkpoints by replaying learning traces and assessment records, and it serves both as a feature-extraction substrate and as an explanation-grounding substrate. Predictive features are derived through graph-mediated queries, while features, attributions, alerts, evidence items, and raw records are represented as queryable graph entities. The framework is instantiated and evaluated on a public learning-analytics benchmark under a temporal protocol. The results show that graph-mediated feature extraction preserves the predictive behavior of equivalent raw-table features across model families and checkpoints. Generated alerts are materialized as evidence chains linking risk decisions to feature attributions, evidence items, and raw platform records. The study shows that early-warning prediction can be routed through a semantic and provenance-aware representation while preserving predictive performance and adding traceability, verifiability, and evidence-grounded explanation.

Web-based learning platforms continuously record learner activity, including resource accesses, submissions, scores, registration events, assessment results, and withdrawals. Learning analytics has built on these traces to develop early-warning systems that estimate, before the end of a course, which learners may be at risk of failing or dropping out [1, 12]. Such systems can support timely pedagogical intervention, but their usefulness depends on more than predictive accuracy. For an alert to be actionable, instructors also need to understand which learning traces, assessment events, or temporal patterns justify the risk signal.

The predictive dimension of early-warning learning analytics is now relatively well served. Tree-based ensembles, gradient-boosting methods, and neural architectures can achieve strong discrimination when trained on interaction and assessment features [19, 31]. However, the explanatory status of the resulting alerts remains limited. In a typical pipeline, raw platform logs are transformed into tabular features, a predictive model assigns a risk score, and a post-hoc attribution method such as SHAP [24] may indicate that an engineered variable, for example total_clicks, contributed to the prediction. Such feature-level explanations are useful for model inspection, but they often stop short of what instructors need for pedagogical interpretation and action. An instructor-facing alert should not only indicate that a learner is at risk; it should also make explicit which learning evidence supports this claim. A feature attribution names an engineered quantity, but it does not necessarily identify the concrete learning events behind it: which interactions decreased, which assessment was missed, which raw records substantiate the alert, and whether the explanation can be queried, traced, or contested. This creates a gap between predictive performance and evidence-grounded interpretability, a limitation emphasized in explainable learning analytics and AI-in-education research [17].

The central design principle is that the graph is not a post-hoc explanatory layer added after prediction; instead, it acts as the operational substrate for feature construction, prediction, attribution representation, and evidence verification. At each checkpoint, learner feature vectors are extracted from the twin using a graph-mediated query catalogue and passed to an early-warning classifier. The framework is later instantiated and evaluated on the Open University Learning Analytics Dataset (OULAD) [19].

papers.title: Conservative Policy Iteration For Zero-Sum POSGs
papers.abstract: Occupancy-state reductions make dynamic programming possible for zero-sum partially observable stochastic games (zs-POSGs). Existing point-based solvers usually optimise a central value function. This restores Bellman recursion, but it requires point-based updates over high-dimensional occupancy spaces. We introduce an approximate policy-iteration algorithm for finite-horizon zs-POSGs. The method maintains one policy per player and updates both jointly along occupancy trajectories induced by conservative policy updates. Instead of approximating a full central value function, each update uses a single supporting hyperplane induced by the current joint policy. The algorithm alternates local policy improvements, conservative updates, and persistent exploration. Computation is therefore concentrated on occupancy regions where the current joint policy is exploitable. On finite-horizon zero-sum POSG benchmarks, the method is competitive at small horizons and often improves the runtime-exploitability trade-off at larger horizons compared with PBVI, HSVI, and CFR+.

papers.intro:
Planning under imperfect information requires agents to act from histories rather than from the true state. In partially observable Markov decision processes (POMDPs), belief states restore a Markovian dynamic program and support exact and point-based solvers (Aström, 1965; Smallwood and Sondik, 1973; Sondik, 1978; Pineau et al., 2003; Smith and Simmons, 2004). In partially observable stochastic games (POSGs), partial observability is coupled with strategic uncertainty. Each player must reason about the hidden state, its own information, and the possible information and actions of the other players (Hansen et al., 2004; Kovařík et al., 2022). The two-player zero-sum case, called a zero-sum partially observable stochastic game (zs-POSG), is the adversarial form of this problem. Dynamic programming is classical for fully observable stochastic games (Shapley, 1953; Filar and Vrieze, 1997), but partial observability requires a sufficient statistic for planning. Common-information, plan-time, and occupancy-state reductions provide such statistics for decentralised control and Dec-POMDPs (Nayyar et al., 2013; Dibangoye et al., 2013; Dibangoye et al., 2016b; Oliehoek, 2013). Recent work has extended this programme to adversarial settings, including value-structure results, one-sided partially observable stochastic games, public-observation games, and general two-player zs-POSGs (Wiggers et al., 2016; Horák et al., 2017; Horák and Bošanský, 2019; Kartik and Nayyar, 2019; Buffet et al., 2020; Delage et al., 2023; Sokota et al., 2023; Escudie et al., 2025). In these reductions, a zs-POSG is lifted to an occupancy stochastic game. The lifted state is a distribution over hidden states and histories. The lifted actions are decision rules. The reduced game is fully observed by the planner. It preserves the value of the original game and restores Bellman recursion.

The two policies are updated together, so the opposing policy used during rollouts is supplied by the other player-specific planning process. papers.title: GUI-JEPA: Candidate-Conditioned JEPA Latents as a Fast Action Policy for Mobile GUI Agents
papers.abstract: Mobile GUI agents are typically fine-tuned 7B-scale vision-language models (VLMs) that generate each action as text. However, these VLMs decode every action token by token, and even agents that score candidate actions keep a large language model or VLM in the loop, making them slow and memory-hungry. To address these issues, we propose GUI-JEPA, to our knowledge the first decoder-free GUI agent policy built on a Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA), which selects actions in the latent space of a JEPA encoder pretrained on unlabelled GUI screenshots. Its action- and region-conditioned latent predictor turns the screen latent into one latent per candidate action, letting lightweight heads score all candidates against the instruction in a single batched pass, without decoding a token. We further show that the scorer relies on this latent pathway and that the predictor is trained for the decision itself: a randomly initialised predictor does just as well as one pretrained on screen dynamics. On AndroidControl, GUI-JEPA is 2.8-4.0x faster on the same GPU than a Qwen2.5-VL-7B agent we fine-tune with the same inputs, while reaching 86-92% of its in-distribution accuracy with 6% of its parameters. Code is available at https://github.com/bcwang-sjtu/GUI-JEPA

A mobile graphical user interface (GUI) agent’s per-step cost is dominated by a 7B+ vision-language model (VLM) decoding its action token by token. On one NVIDIA H20, a Qwen2.5-VL-7B agent (Bai et al., 2025) LoRA-fine-tuned (Hu et al., 2022) on AndroidControl needs 207 ms per step under vLLM (Kwon et al., 2023) and 507 ms under Hugging Face (HF) transformers to emit a JSON action of ∼{\sim}12 tokens (median over 100 real steps, batch 1; Table 3), and 8B-class agents average 2.6–10.6 s per step in a live-device benchmark (Sui et al., 2026). Yet in GUI grounding a VLM fixes its target elements during prefill, with decoding only refining coordinates (Lin et al., 2026a), and decoding on the critical path makes agents correct but late (Dong et al., 2026). Could a GUI agent score its actions in the latent space of a joint-embedding predictive architecture (Assran et al., 2023, JEPA;), without decoding them at all?

papers.title: Aligning Institutional Power and Operational Ability
papers.abstract: To be socially sustainable, Agentic AI systems require normative designs that align responsibilities with the ability to fulfil them. Identifying incongruences such as unsatisfiable expectations or privilege escalation is crucial in avoiding normative pitfalls. In this study, we discuss design dimensions suitable for describing multi-agent systems in light of this norm-ability alignment requirement. We propose a formal framework centred on process-oriented modelling and institutional power for the analysis of a given normatively relevant process, discuss strategies for repairing it, and elaborate on how the symmetrical relation between operational process and institutional state affects the lifecycle of normative positions.

papers.intro:
Social systems come with social expectations and responsibilities ascribed to the participating actors. However, if we do not align those with the concrete ability to perform the actions required by those expectations, we enter into an incongruent state of affairs that might render somebody else’s rights vacuous – or better, their exercise frustrated – even without incurring any explicit norm-violation. For instance, if an individual is legally granted freedom of movement in a building while barriers prevent them from ever leaving the facility, their right is formally acknowledged yet materially nullified. Previous work, such as [30], started investigating the interaction between deontic and potestative concepts, showing how an instrumental interpretation of the latter towards the former can reveal gaps in institutional design, while distinguishing the two concepts as belonging to two distinct ontological categories.

In the context of artificial multi-agent systems, including those currently described as Agentic AI, such incongruence may hinder their controllability. This issue can become apparent even in localised settings, as suggested by the diverging industrial approaches to software development-oriented agentic harnesses such as Claude Code [1], Codex [21], or Pi [7]. As highlighted by recent episodes like the OpenAI incident involving the Hugging Face platform in July 2026 [22, 13], agents authorised to use tools for a task may exploit sequences of operational effects to gain access beyond the boundaries intended by system designers. Conversely, assigning tasks to harnessed agents that do not have access to the required operational machinery (e.g., Model Context Protocol (MCP) connections) could result in ineffective orchestration at best, and mission-critical failure at worst. In the interest of designing systems that outline a clear liability structure and support socially sustainable governance of agentic artificial intelligence, it is crucial that we avoid such normative pitfalls.

Although historically many computational normative frameworks have remained primarily deontic-centric, several explicitly represent institutional power alongside obligations and permissions, including [2, 6, 32, 33]. Especially in computational settings, operational ability becomes a precondition for sound attribution of institutional power and deontic positions alike; that is, powers and duties become highly problematic in a world where their corresponding actions cannot be performed [31]. In this context, we observe that tracing institutional side-effects remains difficult as long as the operational layer lacks an adequate process model-oriented execution semantics. The main function of this formalism would be to capture action-dependence (see e.g. [5]) in workflows. Moreover, we argue for treating power as an independent normative category in its institutional, constitutively-ascribed form [10, 14] and “instrumental” but ontologically distinct interpretation i.e., to maintain or update the state of normative systems [30]. Failing to do so hinders the ability to identify some undesirable configurations such as lingering powers and unsatisfiable obligations (see section 4). Such misalignments may give rise to disputes requiring judicial intervention ex-post, motivating their identification and prevention at design time.

The scenario is loosely inspired by a real consignment dispute [16] over a Star Wars Lego collection entrusted to a franchise that later changed hands, with the consignor alleging that neither payment nor the goods were returned. It is a simplification to illustrate our model, as we assume the consigned goods fall into BB’s estate on insolvency, and that BB’s mandate to sell lapses on insolvency. It is not within our scope to model real consignment law here. The consigned goods represent a contested resource, preconditioning normative actions and enabling operational continuation of the process in alternative directions.

papers.title: Clearing the FoG: Training KG Agents to Retrieve the Evidence Behind Their Answers
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can answer many factual questions correctly, but a correct answer is not necessarily a supported one. For an LLM agent, a knowledge graph (KG) plays two roles: as a source of answers, it supplies facts that the model lacks; as a source of evidence, it supplies the supporting triples that make an answer traceable and auditable. However, existing KG agents treat the KG only as a source of answers: their training data carries answers but not evidence, and their training rewards check the answer but not the retrieved evidence, so agents often answer correctly without retrieving the supporting triples. We propose FoG, a framework that trains KG agents to retrieve the evidence behind their answers. FoG consists of evidence-grounded synthesis, a KG interaction agent, and an evidence-coverage process reward (ECPR): the synthesis recursively hides explicit entities behind verifiable sub-questions, so that every question carries its supporting triples by construction; the agent records the triples returned by the KG; and ECPR credits each supporting triple to the turn that first retrieves it. Experiments on three KGQA benchmarks demonstrate that FoG enables 3B--4B open-source agents to outperform substantially larger baselines in answer accuracy and evidence coverage, with zero-shot cross-KG transfer.

(2024), where users need evidence that they can check Sui et al. (2025); Agrawal et al. (2024). Current LLM answers thus lie in a fog: the answer is visible, yet the evidence behind it remains hidden.

Knowledge graphs (KGs) Pan et al. (2024) offer a natural way to clear this fog, since they store facts as verifiable triples. Existing KG-augmented methods follow two paradigms (Figure 2). Retrieval-based methods (Luo et al., 2024; Li et al., 2025; Luo et al., 2025) retrieve triples, paths, or subgraphs and answer from them. Agent-based methods (Sun et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2024; Lin et al., 2025; Jiang et al., 2025) interact with the KG through a multi-turn “think–act–observe” process, and recent work trains them with reinforcement learning (RL) (Lin et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025; Sun et al., 2025; Sun et al., 2026a).

An LLM with no KG access can already answer many benchmark questions correctly, and even an RL-trained agent can answer correctly while retrieving only part of the supporting triples. We identify two causes. First, training data carries answers but not evidence: most KGQA datasets annotate answers and at most logical forms Talmor and Berant (2018); Yih et al. (2016); Gu et al. (2021), and recovering the supporting triples afterwards requires enumerating and verifying paths for every question. Second, training rewards check the answer but not the evidence: most rewards score only the final answer or whether the KG returns it Lin et al. (2025); Song et al. (2026); Xu et al. (2026); Chen et al. (2025); Sun et al. (2025), so a trajectory that reaches the answer through part of the evidence earns as much as one that retrieves all of it. The process rewards that go further depend on an LLM judge or on gold paths recovered for every question Wang and Yu (2026a); Yan et al. (2026), both of which are costly. Both causes trace back to one bottleneck: evidence is expensive to recover once a question has been written.

To remove this bottleneck, we propose FoG (Figure 1), a framework that trains KG agents to retrieve the evidence behind their answers. Our key observation is that evidence is hard to recover after a question is written but can be embedded when the question is constructed and then rewarded during training. First, evidence-grounded synthesis recursively hides the explicit entities of a seed question behind verifiable sub-questions, so every question carries its supporting triples. Second, a KG interaction agent answers through multi-turn KG queries and records every triple that the KG returns. Lastly, during RL training, an evidence-coverage process reward (ECPR) gives a dense reward to each turn that first retrieves one of these supporting triples. papers.title: GraphRAGProv: GraphRAG Meets How-Provenance
papers.abstract: GraphRAG systems often use knowledge graphs to retrieve relevant context for an LLM that produces the final answer. That makes answers more inscrutable and therefore less appealing for domains where transparency is paramount. We present GraphRAGProv, an architecture that executes SPARQL queries over source-grounded RDF graphs to compute answers and their how-provenance polynomials. These polynomials record which statement occurrences were used and how they were combined. Because each occurrence is linked to its source text, users can follow these links to check whether the extracted statements reflect the text and whether the query combines them to answer the question. Querying thereby becomes a way to inspect and evaluate the text-to-graph transformation. Our interactive demo examines 400 cases from two multi-hop QA benchmarks, revealing extraction and query errors even when the final answer is correct.

authors.name: Luis Galarraga
authors.institution: Centre National de la Recherche Scientifique

papers.intro:
GraphRAG uses graph structure to connect information across a corpus of text. Microsoft GraphRAG builds entity relation graphs and community summaries, while HippoRAG builds an OpenIE graph and uses Personalized PageRank for retrieval (Edge et al., 2024; Gutiérrez et al., 2024). In many such architectures, the graph determines what evidence reaches an LLM, but the LLM still produces the final answer. A retrieved path or subgraph may therefore show what evidence was available to the LLM without specifying how the returned value was computed. This is limiting in critical settings such as medical diagnosis or computational justice, where the computation leading to an answer may itself need to be verified.

GraphRAG uses graph structure to connect information across a corpus of text. Microsoft GraphRAG builds entity relation graphs and community summaries, while HippoRAG builds an OpenIE graph and uses Personalized PageRank for retrieval (Edge et al., 2024; Gutiérrez et al., 2024). In many such architectures, the graph determines what evidence reaches an LLM, but the LLM still produces the final answer. A retrieved path or subgraph may therefore show what evidence was available to the LLM without specifying how the returned value was computed. This is limiting in critical settings such as medical diagnosis or computational justice, where the computation leading to an answer may itself need to be verified.

One approach is to produce the answer by querying the graph itself. This requires representing facts from the text documents as explicit statements in a data graph, such as subject-predicate-object triples in RDF. A question can then be translated into SPARQL and evaluated by a graph database engine, so that the query result is the final answer (Lan et al., 2021; Peng et al., 2025). While this approach is well established when a knowledge graph already exists (Lan et al., 2021; Feng et al., 2025), applying it to document collections requires constructing the graph from text first, as in Neo4j’s LLM Graph Builder (Neo4j Labs, 2024) and KAG (Liang et al., 2025). KAG reports answering questions from retrieved subgraphs in 33%, 34%, and 18% of cases on HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, and MuSiQue, respectively, and supplements graph reasoning with text retrieval when it yields no results. GraphRAGProv instead uses an LLM to translate questions into SPARQL, with the returned bindings constituting the answers and no text retrieval or LLM generation as a fallback. To make these computations inspectable, we augment query evaluation with database how-provenance (Green et al., 2007), which identifies the contributing statements and records how they were combined. The database computes both the answers and their derivations, without requiring an LLM to interpret retrieved context. Each returned binding is annotated with a polynomial over statement identifiers: multiplication records joint use, while addition records alternative derivations. NPCS (Asma et al., 2024) computes these annotations by query rewriting over reified RDF statements.

A derivation identifies the statements used to compute an answer, but does not establish whether those statements are supported by the source text. GraphRAGProv makes this interpretation inspectable by preserving each extraction as a statement occurrence linked to its source passage and evidence spans. The extractor supplies quotations for the subject, predicate, and object; a deterministic localizer resolves them to exact character spans, and RDF-star reification preserves the occurrence identifier and its source links. NPCS (Asma et al., 2024) uses these identifiers in provenance polynomials, so following a factor recovers both the assertion used in the computation and the original text against which that assertion can be checked.

papers.title: Timestral
papers.abstract: We introduce Timestral, a family of four time series foundation models for probabilistic forecasting, with 5M, 28M, 123M, and 209M parameters. Timestral sets a new state of the art on GIFT-Eval, TIME, and fev-bench, where Timestral-209M and Timestral-123M take the top two places on every metric. We achieve this with three ingredients: Decoupled Horizon Forecasting (DHF), which separates prediction tokens from the causally encoded context, so that longer horizons are trained without masking context and each observed value is both a forecast target and context for later forecasts; a covariate framework that natively supports known-future covariates within a causal architecture; and a two-stage pipeline that pretrains exclusively on a diverse, large-scale synthetic corpus before post-training on a mix of real and synthetic data with extended context. This report describes the model design and its benchmark results. Weights for all four models are available on Hugging Face and inference code on GitHub.
papers.intro:
\Acp tsfm enable forecasting across datasets and domains without retraining. By training on large collections of real and synthetic time series, these models provide a shared alternative to fitting a separate model for each forecasting problem (Ansari et al., 2024; Das et al., 2024). Recent advances have improved forecast accuracy, demonstrated gains from scaling, and extended support to multivariate series and external covariates (Khwaja et al., 2026; Ansari et al., 2025; Podest et al., 2026; Meyer et al., 2026). These developments place increasing importance on how models use the information available at each forecast origin and on the training distributions that support this use.

Recent advances have improved forecast accuracy, demonstrated gains from scaling, and extended support to multivariate series and external covariates (Khwaja et al., 2026; Ansari et al., 2025; Podest et al., 2026; Meyer et al., 2026). Bidirectional encoder-only models such as Chronos-2 and Falcon-2.0 (Ansari et al., 2025; Xia et al., 2026) sample a context length and a horizon length for each training example, so each forward pass covers a single combination of the two. Causal decoder-only models instead forecast from every position of a sequence and thus cover many context lengths in one forward pass. To also cover multiple horizon lengths, recent causal models are trained to forecast several patches ahead directly rather than autoregressively. cpm (cpm), used in TiRex, Toto-2.0, and TimesFM-3 (Auer et al., 2025; Khwaja et al., 2026; Jain and Sen, 2026), achieves this by masking spans of the input sequence. The masked observations, however, are then also unavailable as context for later forecasts in the same training sequence, coupling the horizon distribution to full-patch context masking. Known-future covariates pose a second challenge: their future values must be accessible to forecasts, while future target values must remain hidden.

papers.title: Your Agent Acts Differently When You're Around: How User Presence Changes Agent Behavior in Negotiation
papers.abstract: LLM agents increasingly interact with other agents on behalf of users, yet how users in the loop affect their agents' behavior--for better or worse--remains poorly understood. We study this question through the lens of negotiation, where agents must represent users while strategically bargaining with other agents. To isolate the effect of user presence, we develop PRESENT, a controlled evaluation framework that compares negotiation settings with and without an interactive user, while holding the game, objectives, and user preferences fixed across conditions. Across 11.2k runs spanning 7 games and 8 models, we find that user presence significantly changes both outcomes and behavior. Specifically, negotiation parties with a user obtain higher payouts (+13.7% on average) and their agents negotiate more aggressively. Surprisingly, user presence also induces misaligned behavior, both toward counterparties (where its rate roughly doubles) and toward users (where it emerges in 14.3% of games). These misaligned behaviors are uncorrelated with outcomes and persist even when the user sends only templated, neutral messages. These findings expose two blind spots in current evaluation practice: static instructions miss behaviors that emerge only when users are present, and outcome-level metrics cannot detect them.

LLM-based agents are increasingly deployed to act on behalf of users in interactions with other parties Databricks (2026). In these agent-to-agent settings, agents communicate and negotiate with other agents on tasks such as scheduling, customer service, and purchasing with minimal human supervision Liu et al. (2025b); Cheng et al. (2025); Troy et al. (2026). In practice, the user often remains involved through the task by checking in, steering, or approving their agent’s decisions. (2026); Jain et al. (2026). Conversely, evaluations of agent-agent settings often leave the user out of the interaction entirely; the agent receives a static description of the user’s preferences and is then left to act alone Payne et al. While static instructions specify user preferences, an actual user in the loop also provides feedback, influences the agent’s decisions, and is influenced in turn. Studies of human representatives suggest that the presence and involvement of those they represent can shape not only their strategic behavior (Klimoski and Ash, 1974; Ben-Yoav and Pruitt, 1984), but also the prevalence of inappropriate conduct (Aaldering et al., 2020). This raises the question of whether similar effects arise in LLM agents that act on behalf of users, either towards other agents or users themselves.

For instance, agents may pressure users to accept offers without justification, or more frequently hallucinate and misreport facts to counterparties. papers.title: CohortFlow: A Steerable Clinical Cohort Curation Agent with Localized Semantic Correction
papers.abstract: Language model agents for clinical cohort curation should accommodate evolving eligibility criteria without repeatedly processing unchanged requirements. We introduce CohortFlow, a steerable agent that represents natural language corrections as localized updates to a structured cohort specification and reconciles them with a persistent execution graph. Explicitly recorded semantic dependencies enable affected computations to be selectively invalidated while preserving valid prior results. On 100 scenarios derived from clinical-trial eligibility criteria, comprising 126 correction turns, localized steering achieves 77.0% requirement micro-F1 versus 76.4% for full regeneration using the same 8B model, a small numerical advantage that is not statistically significant ($p=0.493$). It reduces mean correction latency by 64.8% after completion and 44.3% during execution, with 38.1% fewer model calls. In a separate proof-of-concept evaluation over MIMIC, all 13 cohort states execute successfully, while correction trajectories demonstrate selective preservation of unaffected computations and recomputation of changed or dependent nodes. Together, these results show that localized semantic steering can substantially reduce correction latency and model calls while maintaining strong requirement-level accuracy.

papers.intro:
Clinical cohort curation is often iterative: an initial set of eligibility criteria may be revised as clinicians inspect intermediate results, clarify intent, or refine the target population. Existing systems increasingly use language models to translate natural language criteria into computable cohort definitions or reason over electronic health records (EHRs) (Yuan et al., 2019; Park et al., 2024; Shi et al., 2024). However, conventional pipelines generally treat a revised request as a new task, potentially repeating interpretation and computation even when most of the existing cohort definition remains unchanged.

Existing systems increasingly use language models to translate natural language criteria into computable cohort definitions or reason over electronic health records (EHRs) (Yuan et al., 2019; Park et al., 2024; Shi et al., 2024). However, conventional pipelines generally treat a revised request as a new task, potentially repeating interpretation and computation even when most of the existing cohort definition remains unchanged.

This limitation becomes particularly important when corrections arrive during execution. A clinician may add an exclusion criterion, modify a laboratory threshold, or revise a temporal relationship after other parts of the cohort have already been processed. Restarting from the revised request discards valid intermediate work, while modifying only the final result risks leaving the execution state inconsistent with the revised intent. Importantly, execution order does not determine semantic dependency: changing an earlier computation need not invalidate later computations that do not depend on it.
