papers.title: When the Critic Falls Behind: Co-Evolving Rubrics and Harnesses for Continual Agent Self-Improvement
papers.abstract: Autonomous agents increasingly depend on harnesses that govern interaction, memory, tools, and execution around large language models (LLMs). While recent work has begun to evolve these harnesses from execution experience, the supervision used to guide evolution often remains relatively static, making it difficult to track changing behavioral weaknesses across rounds and potentially limiting generalization to unseen tasks. To address this issue, we propose RuHarness, a rubric--harness co-evolution framework for continual agent self-improvement. RuHarness continually discovers and reassesses behavioral criteria from execution trajectories, prioritizes the most relevant unresolved weaknesses, and uses them to guide targeted harness updates while keeping the task objective fixed. Extensive experiments across diverse agent tasks and backbone models show that RuHarness outperforms strong harness-evolution baselines, particularly on unseen held-out tasks. Further analyses show that adaptive rubric prioritization tracks shifting weaknesses and supports more sustained improvement and stable generalization across evolution rounds.

Recent work has begun to evolve the harness itself from execution experience, enabling agents to improve without updating model parameters (Zhang et al., 2026a; Lin et al., 2026b; Lee et al., 2026a). While such approaches can yield substantial gains, recent controlled evaluations suggest that these improvements may weaken on unseen tasks (Wang et al., 2026c), raising questions about whether harness optimization produces generalizable improvement.

One challenge behind this limited generalization is that repeated harness optimization may gradually overfit to task-specific failure patterns exposed during evolution (Srikanth et al., 2026). Existing methods optimize harness against task-level feedback, which indicates whether the agent succeeds but provides limited information about the behavioral deficiencies underlying failure (Zhang et al., 2026a). This limitation becomes increasingly important during continual evolution: as the harness improves, previously dominant failures may be mitigated, while subtler or previously unseen failure patterns emerge (Nie et al., 2026). papers.title: What Improves During Pretraining? Tracking Knowledge Acquisition with Point-in-Time Models
papers.abstract: Language models pretrained on web corpora collected over multiple years learn both general and domain-specific knowledge. How these different kinds of knowledge are learned as pretraining progresses remains unclear. Recent point-in-time models trained on web snapshots from different years provide a way to probe how knowledge prevalence varies over time. Using these models, we propose a temporal variability score (TVS), defined as the coefficient of variation of an item's negative log-likelihood across models. A higher score suggests that the knowledge may be less consistently represented across years of web text. We evaluate six benchmarks covering diverse topics using six models from multiple open-source model families. We find that low- and high-TVS items are learned similarly early in training, but high-TVS items improve faster later on. At the end of the pretraining run, high-TVS items outperform low-TVS items in 34 of 36 model-benchmark settings, with an average advantage of 7.3 points of chance-normalized accuracy. This pattern is most robust on knowledge-intensive tasks, even when comparing items of similar difficulty. Our findings reveal differences in how knowledge is learned over the course of pretraining, with temporal variability providing a diagnostic of these learning dynamics beyond aggregate benchmark scores.

Language models improve on a wide range of tasks as pretraining progresses, yet these gains reveal little about the characteristics of the knowledge being learned (Swayamdipta et al., 2020; Chang et al., 2024). We ask how different kinds of knowledge are learned at different stages of pretraining, using their prevalence in training data as a starting point for characterizing these differences.

Language models improve on a wide range of tasks as pretraining progresses, yet these gains reveal little about the characteristics of the knowledge being learned (Swayamdipta et al., 2020; Chang et al., 2024). We ask how different kinds of knowledge are learned at different stages of pretraining, using their prevalence in training data as a starting point for characterizing these differences.

However, measuring how often a fact or concept appears in pretraining data is difficult because the same knowledge can be expressed in many different ways. Corpus search tools such as infini-gram (Xu et al., 2025) count exact textual matches, but these counts depend on the wording of the query. Passages that express the same knowledge in different words may go uncounted, making exact-match frequency an incomplete measure of prevalence.

papers.title: Can LLMs Reliably Grade Olympiad Proofs? A Study of Mathematical Verification with LLMs
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have made remarkable progress on solving competition-level mathematics, yet their ability to verify natural-language mathematical proofs remains relatively underexplored. This gap is especially pronounced for Olympiad-level proofs, which require meticulous assessment of each claim in a long reasoning chain. Current proof verification thus primarily relies on expert inspection, which is costly to scale. In this paper, we present a systematic study of LLM-based verification in this setting. Specifically, we introduce a human-curated dataset of USAMO 2025 candidate solutions with expert grading, and conduct a broad evaluation of existing LLM verifiers across frontier models. We also propose TROJAN, an iterative self-critique pipeline for generating high-fidelity adversarial proofs at scale. Our comprehensive evaluation covers 20 models spanning seven metrics, two prompt styles, three inference methods, and three prompt templates, showing that state-of-the-art models still leave considerable room for improvement. To narrow this gap, we propose MABGrader, a Multi-Armed Bandit framework that reframes grading as arm selection over the discrete score space. MABGrader outperforms the SOTA ProofGrader by 26.4% in Quadratic Weighted Kappa and reduces grading error by 14%. Code and dataset are available at https://github.com/aziksh-ospanov/TROJAN.

papers.title: Grounding LLM Agents in Business Processes: Process-Aware Knowledge Graphs for Reliable Multi-Step Service Invocation
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents that call enterprise APIs must select the correct endpoints, follow process order, use valid payload keys, and choose coded values from predefined lists. However, current retrieval-augmented service discovery treats endpoints independently and therefore misses process and schema constraints. We address this limitation by integrating Open Data Protocol (OData) metadata and Business Process Model and Notation (BPMN) reference processes in a typed property graph. A hybrid retriever identifies candidate endpoints using dense embeddings and follows process edges to retrieve subsequent endpoints. We evaluate the method on 42 enterprise services with process-chain ground truth. For queries with low lexical overlap between the query and downstream entities, it improves Recall@3 by 5.7 points (n=74), with consistent gains across embedding models and cut-offs. It matches dense retrieval on other queries and provides no improvement on OpenAPI services without a process layer, indicating that the gains arise from process structure. We also evaluate an LLM agent on 81 multi-step queries. It completes 38.7% of tasks, compared with 10.3% for a chunk-based baseline. In an elicitation probe, providing valid code lists eliminates invented codes but leaves invalid keys in 46% of write runs. Full typed context reduces invalid calls to 3% (3 of 101 runs), with no invented codes. These results show that exposing process and schema constraints during retrieval improves the reliability of agent-driven API calls.

papers.intro:
Imagine an AI assistant that must arrange a business trip. It has to find a flight, book it, and then reserve a hotel using the booking reference, in that order. Each booking form also has required fields and fixed code lists, such as cabin class or fare type. The assistant can pick the right booking API and still fail: it may invent a fare code, leave out a required reference, or book the hotel before the flight. Such a call fails just as badly as a call to the wrong API. Reliable multi-step automation therefore needs more than the right endpoint. It also needs two kinds of constraints around each call: sequential constraints (what comes next) and parametric constraints (which keys and code values are valid).

It also needs two kinds of constraints around each call: sequential constraints (what comes next) and parametric constraints (which keys and code values are valid).

Enterprise software has the same problem at a much larger scale. Large companies expose thousands of APIs. A typical SAP S/4HANA system, for example, ships hundreds of Open Data Protocol (OData) services, each with many collections, fields, and cross-references. Suppose a developer asks: “create a purchase order for supplier X with a valid status code, then confirm goods receipt.” Choosing the right endpoint is only the first step. The payload keys must match the schema, the coded values must be valid, and the calls must follow the business process. Each of these rules gives a language model a chance to produce a call that looks right but is invalid.

papers.title: Learning Human Sports Motion Feasibility via Quantile Regression on Tracking Data
papers.abstract: We study time-to-arrival (TTA) in sports: the shortest plausible time a player needs to reach an arbitrary location on the pitch given their current kinematic state, estimated as the lower envelope of observed locomotion times. Rather than modeling space ownership through position density estimation or closed-form physics-based models, we cast TTA as a conditional quantile regression problem, estimating the lower quantile of locomotion time so the model learns a player's lower-envelope arrival time. We train the model on optical tracking data from all 64 matches of the PFF FC FIFA World Cup 2022 dataset, and evaluate a lightweight multilayer perceptron against six player-motion models from the literature, re-expressed as TTA predictors, and a learned reachable- hull baseline. Across our evaluation metrics, the MLP consistently outperforms every physics-based baseline. To probe the generality of the learned locomotion model, we further evaluate it on basketball tracking data and a single-game NFL tracking dataset, analyzing the transferability of player motion dynamics across sports. Our project is available at https://github.com/mguti97/TTA-Quantile.

Over the last decade, professional team sports have undergone a shift from box-score event logs to continuous positional tracking. Optical, radar, and GPS systems now record the locations of every player and the ball multiple times per second in sports such as football [40, 20], basketball [36], and American football [19]. Space is the currency of team sports: where a player can be a second from now determines who can receive a pass, who can close a passing lane, and which regions of the pitch or court a team effectively controls. Almost every method that quantifies that (pitch control, off-ball value or pass-probability surfaces) rests, explicitly or implicitly, on a player-motion model: an answer to the question “where can this player get to, and how fast?” The dependence spans sports: recent models of expected passes [2], dangerous accessible space [5], offside control [33] and pressing intensity [4] in football, off-ball value in basketball [49], and safe pass targeting in American football [38] all inherit such a model, typically with a handful of fixed global parameters. Although developed in the context of sports analytics, player-motion models address a more general problem of predicting the future reachability of moving agents under physical constraints [11, 12]. Similar formulations arise in robotics, where autonomous systems must anticipate the motion of humans or other robots for safe navigation and collision avoidance [47, 9], and in autonomous driving for forecasting the reachable regions of surrounding vehicles and pedestrians [27, 22].

Two answers to the previous question dominate the literature. One line derives a reachable region analytically from an equation of motion and then validates or refits that closed form against tracking [35, 48, 30]. These models are interpretable and cheap, but they commit in advance to a fixed functional form with a handful of global parameters. A second line keeps a continuous notion of space but drops arrival time altogether, shaping a hand-set Gaussian influence kernel around a player’s velocity and position [16, 49] or fitting a kernel-density estimate over observed endpoints [6, 28, 43]. The kernel bandwidth may now be fit from data, but the output is a density or a behavioral commitment likelihood, not a feasibility bound: a location scores high because players are often there, or often choose it, independent of whether anyone could actually get there in time.

We take a complementary, data-driven view that keeps that question central. We directly predict the minimum time-to-arrival (TTA) from a player’s kinematic state to any target location, and we learn it as a quantile of observed locomotion. The key modeling choice is to estimate a low envelope of arrival times rather than the mean: a player may dawdle to any location, so the upper tail is uninformative, but the floor on how quickly they can plausibly arrive is sharply defined and is exactly the quantity downstream space models need. We estimate this floor at τ=0.01\tau=0.01 rather than a looser quantile, since the target quantity is a feasibility bound (the player could be there in time). This turns an ill-posed counterfactual into a well-posed conditional-quantile regression problem. Unlike the iterative pursuit simulations and optimization-based fits some physical models require, the resulting predictor is a single compact feed-forward pass that runs comfortably beyond real time.

papers.title: LoRA on a Budget: Function-Aware Post-Hoc Compression for Adapter Fleets
papers.abstract: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) has become a key mechanism for efficiently specializing foundation models into many task- and user-specific variants. Serving many LoRA adapters under a shared resource budget turns post-hoc compression into a two-level allocation problem: rank must be distributed across layers within each adapter and across adapters within the fleet. Although trained LoRAs contain substantial spectral redundancy, spectral reconstruction alone does not determine how much compression an adapter can functionally tolerate. We formulate fleet compression through a functional rank-distortion frontier for each adapter, followed by fleet-level minimax allocation under a shared rank budget. Given exact frontiers, this decomposition is equivalent to joint optimization over all layer ranks. We introduce Functional Rank Allocation (FRA), an unlabeled method for constructing practical frontiers. FRA measures isolated module truncations end to end, uses these measurements as an additive search surrogate solved by dynamic programming, remeasures every complete candidate, and takes the lower-risk envelope with a complementary spectral proposal before exact minimax allocation over the constructed frontiers. Across 78 adapters from three public fleets, FRA improves worst-case and tail utility over uniform spectral compression in constrained-budget regimes. Fixed-budget probes show that isolated costs rank candidates well, but their calibration shifts across proposal shapes; end-to-end verification and the spectral proposal therefore limit functional-search error.

Foundation models are increasingly adapted into specialized models for a wide range of downstream tasks. Updating every parameter of these models, however, is costly to train, store, and deploy, particularly when many task-specific variants share the same foundation model. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) addresses this cost by learning only a small set of task-specific parameters while leaving the pretrained model frozen. Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) [Hu et al., 2022] has emerged as an especially effective form of PEFT. Rather than modifying a weight matrix directly, LoRA learns an additive update represented as the product of two low-rank factors. This parameterization can retain the benefits of task-specific fine-tuning with far fewer trainable and stored parameters, making each specialization a compact adapter that can be shared, composed with a common base model, and loaded on demand.

papers.title: Polarity--Time Interaction and Multi-Level Reliability for Event-Based Spacecraft Pose Estimation
papers.abstract: Sparse event responses produce uneven keypoint errors whose effects on spacecraft pose depend on correspondence geometry and the reliability of successive observations. We present a reliability-aware framework connecting polarity--time localization, geometric recovery, event--CAD refinement, and trajectory optimization. A three-branch representation combines positive events, negative events, and recent-event timing through cross-branch attention and gating, followed by spatiotemporal aggregation. An ordered semantic-point head estimates relative correspondence precision for geometrically constrained pose recovery. Event-edge and CAD-projection agreement then guide local pose refinement under keypoint-geometry safeguards. At the sequence level, a ten-dimensional descriptor combines heatmap shape, reprojection consistency, and geometric conditioning to set time-aligned observation scales. On the official SPADES challenge test set, the complete system achieves a combined pose score of 0.0474, approximately 5.4\% below PASAN+IRIS. Validation ablations reduce the score from 0.0772 for base localization with uniform PnP to 0.0514 for the complete cascade; on identical single-frame observations, quality weighting reduces the score from 0.0549 with constant-weight optimization to 0.0514.

papers.intro:
Non-cooperative spacecraft pose estimation provides relative geometric information for rendezvous and docking, on-orbit inspection, and space servicing. Given a target CAD model, a vision system can localize semantic keypoints and recover rotation and translation from two-dimensional-to-three-dimensional correspondences. Illumination changes, shadows, and missing local structure make the quality of these observations spatially nonuniform. An event camera asynchronously reports the location, polarity, and time of brightness changes, providing fine-grained temporal measurements for dynamic targets [1]. Pose-estimation methods must therefore operate on sparse spatial responses whose distribution changes with motion.

Research on event-based spacecraft pose estimation has addressed event representation, geometric recovery, and temporal processing. SPADES established a dataset and evaluation baselines [2]. Polarity decoupling and spatiotemporal aggregation organize localization evidence across adjacent event windows [3], while keypoint-based initialization can be connected to model-projection matching and kinematic smoothing [4]. Other work has studied compact event representations and neuromorphic deployment [5]. Together, these studies show that event-based localization can establish semantic correspondences through learned features and constrain pose through known geometry and temporal relationships.

papers.title: MedConstBench: Benchmarking How Constitutions Steer LLMs in Medical Ethics
papers.abstract: As large language models advance rapidly, they are increasingly used to answer medical questions, and many such models are now deployed locally. Once a model is deployed, its behavior is governed mainly by the ethical policy written into its constitution. However, most existing work focuses on factual correctness rather than the trade-off between competing ethical values. Even benchmarks that do evaluate ethics treat it as a fixed property of the model rather than as a variable, so how a constitution reshapes medical-ethics behavior remains largely unexplored. We introduce MedConstBench, a medical-ethics benchmark that treats the deployment constitution as a controlled variable, is organized around Beauchamp's four principles, and is scored by human-calibrated multi-model peer review. It includes MedDilemma, our own dataset of clinical dilemmas, and supports a systematic analysis of how constitutions steer LLMs. Evaluating ten open-source LLMs under four constitutions, we find that the effect of a constitution is dimension-selective and model-dependent, and that no constitution is universally optimal. Motivated by these findings, we propose a do-no-harm adaptive selector that chooses a constitution per model, matching the per-model oracle while guaranteeing a worst-case floor and generalizing to unseen models at low cost.

While some work has begun to evaluate LLMs on medical tasks, it largely focuses on knowledge correctness [14, 15, 16]. By contrast, the ethical behavior of these models has received far less attention. The few studies that address it tend to treat ethics as an intrinsic property of the model, rather than as something shaped by the policy given at deployment [17, 18]. Such evaluations also typically rely on a single LLM as the judge [18], which readily injects its own preferences into the scores and makes the conclusions hard to trust [19]. In practice, however, a deployed model can rarely be retrained, and its ethical behavior is governed mainly by the policy written into the system prompt, commonly referred to as a constitution [20]. This naturally raises our research question. How does a constitution reshape a model’s behavior across ethical dimensions, does it benefit all models equally, and can it backfire?

To comprehensively evaluate the medical-ethics behavior of locally deployable LLMs, we propose MedConstBench, a medical-ethics benchmark organized around Beauchamp’s four principles [21]. At its core is MedDilemma, our dataset of clinical dilemmas with conflicting principles, which targets ethical decision-making rather than factual recall. To test the generalization of our findings, we additionally evaluate on the public MedEthicsQA [22], so that the study spans both clinical decision-making and ethical discourse. Figure 1 illustrates our pipeline. Each item is answered by a set of widely used open-source models under three representative constitutions plus a baseline with no constitution. Scoring open-ended ethical responses is inherently subjective [23]. To remove the bias of any single evaluator, MedConstBench adopts multi-model peer review, in which each response is independently scored by the other models against the four principles (autonomy, non-maleficence, beneficence, justice), and the ratings are aggregated into one score per principle. Calibrated against a human gold standard, multi-model peer review correlates with human judgment substantially better than a single judge, making it a trustworthy measurement instrument.

papers.title: OA-RAG: Ontology-based Agentic RAG for Faithful LLM Reasoning
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) perform well across many real-world tasks but remain prone to hallucination, limiting their reliability in domains such as biomedicine and healthcare, where answers must be grounded in established knowledge. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) mitigates this problem by incorporating external information, but often overlooks logical relationships and relies heavily on the LLM's own reasoning, which can compromise answer faithfulness. We propose OA-RAG, an agent that integrates formal reasoning with LLM reasoning, drawing on both the logical structure and informal annotations of domain ontologies. For each answer, OA-RAG reports the ontology observations used as evidence and a model-assessed grounding level (entailed, supported, related, or unrelated) that characterises the strength of that evidence. Across benchmarks derived from three large-scale ontologies and six real-world medical question-answering tasks, OA-RAG achieves the best overall performance among the evaluated ontology-fine-tuned and popular RAG methods, with particularly strong results on reasoning-intensive tasks. The reported grounding levels also offer a useful indication of answer reliability, with stronger grounding generally associated with higher accuracy. Finally, our results demonstrate the value of ontologies as knowledge sources: OA-RAG is competitive with, and sometimes outperforms, domain-specific RAG systems that draw on sources such as textbooks.

papers.intro:
Ontology-Grounded LLM Reasoning

Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities across a wide range of knowledge-intensive tasks. However, their answers remain constrained by the knowledge encoded in their parameters and may contain hallucinations, that is, plausible but factually incorrect statements (Ji et al., 2023; Huang et al., 2025). Their reliability is further limited by the lack of transparent reasoning and by gaps in domain- or organization-specific knowledge.

However, their answers remain constrained by the knowledge encoded in their parameters and may contain hallucinations, that is, plausible but factually incorrect statements (Ji et al., 2023; Huang et al., 2025). Their reliability is further limited by the lack of transparent reasoning and by gaps in domain- or organization-specific knowledge.

Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) augments LLMs by prompting with external evidence extracted from documents (Gao et al., 2023), tables (Wang et al., 2024), and knowledge graphs (Luo et al., 2024b), while tool-using agents enable more adaptive, dynamic and autonomous access to such sources (Yao et al., 2023; Schick et al., 2023; Sun et al., 2024; Ma et al., 2025). However, existing methods mainly leverage textual and structured knowledge, leaving explicit logical knowledge under-utilised. Consequently, logical inference still relies heavily on the LLM’s internal reasoning, which can make its conclusions less faithful to the given knowledge.

Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) augments LLMs by prompting with external evidence extracted from documents (Gao et al., 2023), tables (Wang et al., 2024), and knowledge graphs (Luo et al., 2024b), while tool-using agents enable more adaptive, dynamic and autonomous access to such sources (Yao et al., 2023; Schick et al., 2023; Sun et al., 2024; Ma et al., 2025). However, existing methods mainly leverage textual and structured knowledge, leaving explicit logical knowledge under-utilised. Consequently, logical inference still relies heavily on the LLM’s internal reasoning, which can make its conclusions less faithful to the given knowledge.

Meanwhile, many scientific and biomedical domains already provide rich shared, explicit and formal knowledge through ontologies in Semantic Web standards like Description Logic underpinned OWL (Web Ontology Language) (Horrocks, 2008; Smith et al., 2007). These ontologies on the Web, such as the Gene Ontology (GO) (Ashburner et al., 2000), FoodOn (Dooley et al., 2018), and SNOMED CT (Donnelly, 2006), encode domain concepts and relations using Description Logic axioms, allowing dedicated reasoners to derive implicit relations soundly and efficiently (Baader et al., 2017b). Moreover, ontologies can contain rich textual annotations, including definitions and comments, providing informal but relatively important and complementary domain knowledge. This combination of formal semantics and textual annotations motivates our central question: Can ontologies bridge formal reasoning and LLM reasoning to produce more faithful answers to domain-specific questions? papers.title: From Structural Feedback to Prompt Policies: Learning Faithful Text-to-Image Prompt Editors
papers.abstract: Prompt optimization should improve the image a user receives without changing the scene the user requested. Yet stylistic rewriting can weaken object attributes and relations even when global text--image similarity remains high. We propose StruPO, a structure-aware prompt editor that uses a calibrated scene graph as a shared representation for policy conditioning and image-grounded supervision. The graph exposes what should be preserved, while deletion, reordering, and insertion provide a token-aligned way to modify the prompt. This turns structural feedback from an external critique into a training signal for a reusable editing policy. Learning from that signal requires handling both uncertain grounding and stochastic image generation. StruPO retains grounding confidence through smooth reward shaping and averages multiple images for each edit before computing group-relative advantages. Experiments span three disjoint 2K-prompt test sets and four frozen generation backbones, with comparisons to learned prompt optimizers, iterative structural feedback, diffusion-model fine-tuning, and inference-time attention control. StruPO improves the faithfulness--aesthetics trade-off, with consistent gains in relational fidelity. Independent automatic evaluators and a 15-annotator study provide complementary evidence, and human preference margins increase with relation complexity. Controlled ablations connect these gains to graph conditioning, local editing, and image-grounded learning. The resulting policy produces reusable optimized text in one pass after graph calibration, without an iterative critique--rewrite loop.

Text-to-image (T2I) models such as Stable Diffusion [1] and DALL-E [2] have made visual content creation widely accessible, but the quality of their outputs still depends strongly on prompt formulation. Users describe what they want to see; generators also respond to how that intent is expressed through composition, lighting, and stylistic detail. Automatic prompt optimization bridges this gap by transforming a user prompt xx into a generator-effective prompt yy. Its objective is twofold: improve the resulting image’s perceptual quality and preserve the scene specified by the user.

This connects the information available when choosing an edit to the object–attribute–relation constraints checked in the generated image. papers.title: The View from Nowhere: Population-Centered Agent Evolution
papers.abstract:
Self-improving AI systems can revise the designs that govern their own behavior. Yet existing approaches center improvement on selected parent agents and their evolutionary experience, leaving the broader population largely underused. We identify a substantial gap between population coverage (i.e., the tasks solved by at least one evolved variant) and the performance of the best individual agent. This gap shows that useful capabilities and diagnostic evidence emerge across the population without being consolidated into its leading agents.
  These observations motivate the view from nowhere, a principle for agent evolution: an agent should be improved by interpreting its behavior through population-wide patterns of success, failure, and prior self-modification. We instantiate this principle as Population-Centered Evolution (PCE). PCE distils task records and modification histories from the population into a population block, which captures recurring failures, complementary successes, and the effects of previously attempted modifications to guide improvements to a selected parent's harness.
  Under matched models, initial harnesses, and evolution schedules, PCE achieves 72.1% success on SWE-bench Verified and 96.7% on Polyglot, improving over a strong group-evolution baseline by 3.2 and 5.9 percentage points. In our evaluation, PCE reduces the gap between population coverage and best-agent performance by one-third on SWE-bench and closes it on Polyglot. These results suggest that treating the population as evidence--not merely as candidates for selection--provides a complementary principle for agent evolution.

papers.intro:
Self-improving AI aims to develop systems that can revise the designs governing their own behavior (Good, 1966; Schmidhuber, 2007). Evolutionary coding agents pursue this goal by modifying their software harnesses while keeping the parameters of their foundation models fixed (Zhang et al., 2026b; Weng et al., 2026; Robeyns et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2026). These harnesses determine how an agent uses the model, tools, feedback, and its environment to solve a task. Through repeated cycles of self-modification and evaluation, these systems generate a growing population of agent variants. The goal is not merely to produce diverse variants, but to turn useful discoveries made during evolution into progressively stronger agents. How to consolidate these discoveries into improvements that persist in leading agents is a central challenge for agent evolution.

How to consolidate these discoveries into improvements that persist in leading agents is a central challenge for agent evolution.

Existing approaches address this challenge through parent selection and experience reuse. The Darwin Gödel Machine (DGM) preserves an archive of agent variants from which future evolution can branch (Zhang et al., 2026b). The Huxley-Gödel Machine (HGM) uses the performance of an agent and its descendants to estimate the potential of continuing that lineage (Wang et al., 2026). Group-Evolving Agents (GEA) selects a small group of parents and allows them to share task records and past self-modifications when proposing improvements (Weng et al., 2026). Despite these differences, the evidence used to propose a modification remains largely parent-local: it comes from the selected parent or parent group rather than from a systematic comparison across the full population. Other variants may remain available for future selection, but their task-level successes, failures, and modification histories do not directly inform the current diagnosis.

We define population coverage as the proportion of tasks solved by at least one evolved variant. As shown in Figure 1a, in one of our GEA runs the evolved population covers 9 more of the 60 held-in tasks than its best individual agent, corresponding to a 15.0 percentage-point gap. This gap shows that successful outcomes remain distributed across the population rather than being fully consolidated into its leading agent. The associated task records allow us to compare variants that succeed and fail on the same task. The population should therefore be treated not only as a pool for parent selection, but also as comparative evidence for deciding how a selected parent should improve.

papers.title: InfraDev: Can Coding Agents Develop AI Infrastructure, and How Can We Tell?
papers.abstract: Coding agents are beginning to develop the production-grade AI infrastructure that trains and serves large models, yet existing benchmarks cover only single kernels or single-GPU tasks, and grade with tests and prompts that misjudge both correct and incorrect patches. We introduce InfraDev, a benchmark of 36 tasks built from real-world pull requests to Megatron-LM, vLLM, and verl, covering infrastructure development for training, inference, and reinforcement learning. Each task asks an agent to reimplement a real change that spans many files and must run correctly across many GPUs. To grade such changes, we jointly synthesize hidden probes, which enforce the requirements the original tests leave unchecked, and a prompt that states every interface the probes call without revealing the solution. We also design a shared execution environment that reuses dependencies and artifacts across tasks, cutting storage by 52-57% and build time by 13-14% on Megatron-LM and vLLM. Across six frontier models, the best resolves only 38.9% of the tasks; the probes reject 32% of the submissions that pass every official test, and with the original pull request descriptions as prompts, no model resolves a single task. Failure analysis shows that structural and state errors dominate and that agents' own tests rarely check memory, time, or traffic. Turning these findings into an agent skill raises the resolved rate of a frontier model on the Megatron-LM tasks by 10.5%.

papers.intro:
Real-world AI infrastructure spans training, inference, and reinforcement learning (Shoeybi et al., 2020; Kwon et al., 2023; Zheng et al., 2024; Sheng et al., 2025). Each is backed by a large codebase that evolves rapidly with new models and hardware: vLLM alone merged 1,918 commits in June 2026, about 64 per day (Luu, 2026). Developing this infrastructure means implementing changes that range from a single GPU kernel to coordinated edits across parallelism, memory, and communication subsystems. Such a change must be correct in two senses. It must be numerically correct, computing the right activations, gradients, and states under distributed execution, and it must be behaviorally correct: a new feature must take effect, and an optimization must actually reduce memory, communication, or time on realistic workloads. Coding agents are beginning to make these changes, as they take on longer and more complex software engineering tasks (Jimenez et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025b; Deng et al., 2025; Kwa et al., 2025). This raises the question: Can coding agents develop real-world AI infrastructure, and how can we tell?

Answering this question requires benchmarks that address three limitations of existing evaluations. First, existing benchmarks have a narrow task scope. Most evaluate individual GPU kernels (Ouyang et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025; Chan et al., 2026; Huang et al., 2026) or single-GPU inference optimization (Nangia et al., 2026; Yeon et al., 2026). Φ\Phi-Bench recently extended the scope to system-level optimization (Ding et al., 2026), but its tasks are optimization problems with fixed targets rather than the changes developers actually ship. Most real infrastructure changes go further: they span many files and modules and must run correctly across many GPUs. Second, reusing a pull request’s own tests and description as the grading suite and task prompt (Jimenez et al., 2024) yields unreliable grading in both directions. The tests are incomplete on both counts. Among the 36 pull requests we study, 24 have no test that checks a numerical result, and 13 of the 15 performance optimizations have no test that checks the promised saving, so a patch that skips the optimization still passes. papers.title: TCM-DiagCommit: A TCM-SD-Derived Benchmark for Evidence-Conditioned Syndrome Selection and Commitment
papers.abstract: Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) syndrome differentiation is usually evaluated as static final-label selection over complete clinical records. This setting hides three diagnostic behaviors: whether a model distinguishes semantic-neighbor syndrome labels from easy random distractors, whether it updates predictions as evidence fields are revealed, and whether it should commit under uncertainty. We introduce TCM-DiagCommit, a benchmark derived from the public TCM-SD/ZY-BERT resource while retaining its source syndrome labels; it converts 1,834 source cases into 23,842 task rows over 148 syndrome labels. The benchmark combines random, profile-neighbor, and full-vocabulary candidate ladders with staged t1/t2/t3 evidence. It also includes fixed-label tongue/pulse perturbations and insufficient-evidence variants. A benchmark-defined action contract scores commit, acquire, defer, and abstain. Across five zero-shot DirectLLM calibrations, random10 top-1 accuracy is 63.2% to 66.4%, but hard20 falls to 24.7% to 30.3% and full148 to 14.8% to 22.3%; on hard20, WT(all) wrong-terminal commits remain 62.2% to 74.3%. These results show that final-answer accuracy alone is insufficient for diagnostic benchmark evaluation: answer selection, evidence use, and benchmark commitment scoring should be measured separately.

Medical QA and diagnosis benchmarks often cast diagnosis as complete-evidence final-answer selection. papers.title: KPPax: preprocess differentiable kinetic ODE for machine learning in atmospheric chemistry
papers.abstract: Atmospheric chemical mechanisms are commonly distributed in the language of the Kinetic PreProcessor (KPP), which generates efficient Fortran or C code but does not fit into the differentiable programming frameworks in which machine-learning models are developed. We present KPPax, a kinetic preprocessor that generates differentiable, just-in-time compiled, and vectorisable chemistry code in JAX from mechanisms written in the KPP language. KPPax evaluates the rate law with sparse operations in log space, which keeps it differentiable, and integrates the stiff system with the implicit solvers and the forward- and reverse-mode adjoints of the \texttt{diffrax} library, so that exact sensitivities are obtained without hand-derived adjoint code. We demonstrate two applications with the POLLU benchmark mechanism. In the first, the Fisher information matrix computed from an automatically differentiated Jacobian predicts, before any fit, which of the 25 rate coefficients a flow-tube-like design can identify, and noisy synthetic estimation confirms the predicted uncertainties of the nine identifiable rate coefficients to within about 30\% while revealing clusters of fast reactions of which only ratios are constrained. In the second, a neural-network correction of an emission inventory is trained offline on per-scenario 4D-Var retrievals and then fine-tuned online through the chemical model, which reduces the error of the biogenic correction by a factor of 2.4--5 and recovers information on low-temperature emissions that the individual retrievals lose. KPPax makes KPP mechanisms directly usable for parameter estimation and hybrid physics--machine-learning modelling.

papers.intro:
Chemicals and aerosols in the ambient air affect human health, weather, and climate (Seinfeld and Pandis, 2016). Their atmospheric concentrations vary strongly in space and time, governed by emission, chemical transformation, aerosol formation, transport by meteorological conditions, and eventual removal by deposition (Brasseur and Jacob, 2017). Comprehensive atmospheric chemical mechanisms, such as the near-explicit Master Chemical Mechanism (Jenkin et al., 1997; Saunders et al., 2003), contain thousands of species coupled through more than ten thousand reactions, and hand-coding the resulting stiff ODE system and its Jacobian is tedious and error-prone.

The Kinetic PreProcessor (KPP) automates this process (Damian et al., 2002). Given a chemical mechanism specified in a dedicated description syntax, the KPP language, KPP parses the reaction list with a Flex/Yacc scanner–parser and generates Fortran or C code that evaluates the time derivative of the concentrations and its Jacobian. The generated code exploits the sparsity of the Jacobian through species reordering and sparse linear algebra routines, which keeps the implicit time stepping required by stiff chemistry efficient, and it is paired with a suite of stiff numerical integrators, including Rosenbrock, BDF, and Runge–Kutta methods. KPP also generates direct-decoupled and adjoint sensitivity code, which efficiently computes derivatives of the model solution with respect to rate coefficients, initial concentrations, and other parameters. These sensitivities support applications such as parameter estimation, uncertainty analysis, and variational data assimilation (Sandu et al., 2003). This tight coupling between mechanism parsing, sparse Jacobian generation, and forward and adjoint sensitivity code generation has made KPP a standard tool in atmospheric chemistry modelling, but it also means that the resulting code inherits the constraints of the Fortran and C environments and of the CPU hardware for which it was designed.

Other tools to preprocess and solve chemical kinetics have been developed for other software and hardware environments. pykpp (Henderson, ) is a preprocessor written in Python, which parses mechanisms written in the KPP language and solves the kinetic ODE with SciPy solvers. PyBox generates 0-dimensional box models that include both atmospheric chemistry and aerosol processes, in which the chemistry is solved by the Assimulo ODE solver (Topping et al., 2018), and PyCHAM reuses the mechanism parsing of PyBox but solves the ODE with SciPy (O’Meara et al., 2021). The Multi-Scale Infrastructure for Chemistry and Aerosols (MUSICA) is implemented in C++ and provides an option to run on accelerators such as GPUs (Pfister et al., 2020). For the EMAC model, a source-to-source tool translates the KPP-generated Fortran code into CUDA kernels to solve the chemical kinetics on GPUs (Alvanos and Christoudias, 2017). TChem-atm couples gas-phase and aerosol chemistry and runs on CPUs and GPUs through the Kokkos performance-portability library, constructing the Jacobian automatically for a range of stiff ODE solvers (Díaz-Ibarra et al., 2026). These developments target the efficient forward simulation of process-based atmospheric models, which are built on explicit physical and chemical processes and are therefore interpretable, since the driving forces in the model can be perturbed to test their influence on the output. However, process-based models are limited by the processes that they do not resolve, and amending the model structure or tuning its parameters against observations remains laborious and computationally expensive.

Data-driven approaches, for example neural networks trained on historical atmospheric observations, offer flexible and fast emulation of atmospheric processes with comparable accuracy. ChemNNE is a neural-network emulator of the atmospheric chemical ODE that is considerably faster than the numerical solver (Liu et al., 2025), and TopoFlow is a topography-aware neural network for high-resolution air-quality prediction (Kheder et al., 2026). Neural networks can also partially solve the estimation of rate coefficients in chemical ODEs (Peng et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2026). However, purely data-driven models often lack interpretability and the ability to predict anomalies or extreme events, and their training is data-intensive and becomes infeasible when observations are sparse. Neural networks are trained by gradient descent, which relies on automatic differentiation, and although this is possible in Fortran, the majority of neural-network models are developed in Julia or in Python frameworks such as PyTorch and JAX.

papers.title: SpectRAG: Weighted Chunk Graphs for Token-Budgeted Context Selection in Multi-Hop Retrieval-Augmented Generation
papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems ground large language models (LLMs) by retrieving external evidence and conditioning generation on the retrieved context. Although dense retrieval is effective for local semantic matching, independently ranked retrieval can return redundant passages, miss cross-chunk dependencies, and provide incomplete evidence for multi-hop reasoning. We propose SpectRAG, a spectral graph-augmented retrieval framework that combines hybrid candidate seeding, weighted chunk graph construction, graph-based expansion, spectral relevance propagation, and token-budgeted context selection. Document chunks are represented by dense semantic embeddings and graph-spectral coordinates derived from a weighted chunk graph whose edges encode semantic similarity, document adjacency, section hierarchy, shared entities, citation links, and similarity between LLM-generated utility questions. At query time, SpectRAG builds a high-recall seed set using exact inner-product search and hybrid relevance signals, expands it over the chunk graph, re-scores candidates using graph proximity and spectral information, and assembles the final context under a fixed token budget. The goal is not merely to retrieve individually similar chunks, but to construct a context that is relevant, diverse, structurally connected, and sufficient for grounded reasoning. Experiments on MultiHopRAG, UltraDomain, and long-document question-answering settings show that SpectRAG improves broad evidence recovery and achieves competitive generation quality against dense, hybrid, HyDE, LightRAG, and NaiveRAG baselines. The results further indicate that graph-spectral structure is particularly useful for inference-oriented and cross-document retrieval, while highlighting trade-offs in early precision, computational cost, and domain-dependent performance.

papers.intro:
Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) has become a practical architecture for grounding large language models (LLMs) in external corpora [1]. In a standard pipeline, documents are chunked, chunks are embedded, a query is embedded, and the top-kk chunks most similar to the query are provided as context to an LLM. Dense passage retrieval [2] and hybrid sparse–dense retrieval are now widely used because they are scalable and effective for local factual lookup. In this paper, we see this constraint as a separation of two paradigms for retrieval. One of them is the classical top-kk paradigm, where chunks are scored based on their individual similarities to the query, and the top-scoring chunks are selected. The other paradigm is called context-set retrieval, where the goal is to find a set of chunks that, together, provide enough evidence for generation. In this paradigm, a good RAG retriever should not only be able to retrieve chunks similar to the query, but also form a cohesive context set. Nevertheless, the method of extracting the top-kk vectors is subject to three recurring limitations. Firstly, given that adjacent or semantically similar passages generally occupy the same region of the embedding space, this method has the potential to eliminate superfluous evidence. Secondly, it may overlook structurally important segments that are necessary for multi-step reasoning, even if they are not immediately close to the query. Thirdly, while this method treats segments as largely independent units, real-world text corpora possess a structure that includes document order, section hierarchy, shared entities, citations, temporal dependencies, and conceptual links [3].

While the standard top-k retrieval method is practically effective, it is limited when the answer requires a context set rather than a group of similar passages. For dense vector retrieval, chunks are usually ranked based on their individual similarity to the query. The success of this ranking mechanism depends on the local representation of the required evidence in only one or a few semantically similar passages. However, many real-world question-answering (QA) and reasoning tasks require evidence distributed across multiple chunks, documents, or sections. In such cases, the most advantageous setting of context may not be composed of the highest-ranked components alone, but of passages that are jointly relevant, complementary, and structurally interconnected [4]–[6].

Retrieval-augmented generation with graphs (GraphRAG)-style approaches represent information as graphs and exploit relational links to support retrieval and generation across connected evidence [6]. Related work has explored entity graphs, document graphs, knowledge graphs, and graph-augmented memory structures. For example, GEM-RAG [22] graphical eigenmemories by tagging data segments with utility questions, connecting them into a graph, and using eigendecomposition to form higher-level memory nodes. CrossAug further highlights that many GraphRAG pipelines miss relations whose supporting evidence spans multiple chunks, and proposes an offline graph-augmentation strategy to recover cross-chunk structure [7]. These studies indicate that retrieval can benefit from modeling both the semantic similarity between a query and individual chunks and the structural relationships among these chunks.

Related work has explored entity graphs, document graphs, knowledge graphs, and graph-augmented memory structures. For example, GEM-RAG [22] graphical eigenmemories by tagging data segments with utility questions, connecting them into a graph, and using eigendecomposition to form higher-level memory nodes. CrossAug further highlights that many GraphRAG pipelines miss relations whose supporting evidence spans multiple chunks, and proposes an offline graph-augmentation strategy to recover cross-chunk structure [7]. These studies indicate that retrieval can benefit from modeling both the semantic similarity between a query and individual chunks and the structural relationships among these chunks.

However, existing graph-enhanced RAG methods often focus on graph construction, entity-level relations, or community-level summarization. The problem of selecting a compact, diverse, and structurally connected context set remains underexplored. A retrieval system for multi-hop and long-document reasoning should, in principle, be designed to satisfy numerous objectives simultaneously. The goals of this initiative are numerous and include, but are not limited to: • To reduce redundancy, resulting in more efficient and varied retrieval strategies and, hence, greater confidence in the ongoing efforts. • Bridge evidence recovery in process. • Ensure structural coherence of the selected segments is very important.

We introduce SpectRAG, a retrieval framework that combines dense candidate seeding with graph-spectral context-set optimization. This framework does not thoroughly replace dense retrieval techniques. Rather, it uses dense vector similarity to generate an initial candidate pool with high recall, then leverages the structure of a weighted chunk graph to refine the final context set. The suggested framework represents chunks using both dense semantic embeddings and spectral coordinates that are derived from the graph Laplacian. These spectral coordinates offer structural insights into the corpus retriever to consider graph connectivity, latent communities, and inter-chunk relationships during the selection process, and enable the retriever to account for graph connectivity, latent communities, and cross-chunk relations during selection.

In the querying stage, SpectRAG converts the user query into embeddings, and then creates a seed set from the embedding space that has high recall. The seed set is then further extended via graph neighborhoods for fetching other related segments that do not necessarily match the query well, but can act as connectors or be evidence itself. The relevance of queries is then propagated to the candidate subgraph that is affected by this, thus making relevance propagate from the matched segments to other related evidence. Finally, SpectRAG applies a token-budgeted context selection stage that assembles the final context under a fixed input budget. This stage prioritizes relevant and structurally connected chunks, preserves a protected core of high-confidence evidence, applies a precision-oriented filtering strategy for lower-ranked candidates, and backfills the remaining budget when necessary to avoid under-utilization of the available context window.

papers.title: The uneven rise of AI-generated web content
papers.abstract: In less than five years, generative artificial intelligence (AI) has dramatically reshaped the public-facing web. Using a sample of more than 5 million crawlable webpages, we demonstrate that the share containing AI-generated text has increased precipitously, but unevenly. Our analyses reveal substantial differences in AI composition across language and domain categories (e.g., .edu, .com, or .gov). A higher fraction of English-language webpages contain AI-generated text compared to pages in other languages, and prevalence is substantially lower on .gov and .edu domains compared to .com. These distinctions persist even after accounting for compositional effects. We also find heterogeneity based on a page's position in the connectivity structure of the web. AI-generated text is most common and has increased most rapidly in pages that are the least central in the graph, which drives much of the overall growth in AI-generated text. A slower increase has taken place for more central pages, with the most central tier emerging as the least likely to contain AI-generated text. Methodologically, we use multiple AI detection tools, and generate estimates using a Bayesian hierarchical model that incorporates corrections for the detectors' statistical properties (both false positives and false negatives) and allows for different detector performance across groups, while propagating uncertainty in detector error rates into prevalence estimates. Our work suggests that AI is a prominent, but varied, contributor to public information and internet-based communication.

papers.intro:
The public web is both a main channel through which institutions, businesses, and individuals communicate and the largest source of text from which language models are trained (Brown et al., 2020; Touvron et al., 2023; Penedo et al., 2024; Baack, 2024). Changes in how text on the web is produced propagate to what people read and to how the next generation of language models learn (Shumailov et al., 2024). Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is now reshaping the text on webpages at a rate that is accelerating and in a manner that is highly heterogeneous. Using a probability sample of 5.1 million pages from the crawlable web from 2019-2026, spanning every language and the full crawlable link graph, together with a Bayesian model that corrects for the false positives and false negatives of multiple AI detectors, we find that in August 2026 about 24 percent (95% credible interval 22.9-24.4) of crawlable webpages contained AI-generated or AI-edited text, and the rate of increase has nearly doubled, from 4.6 percentage points per year between early 2023 and early 2025 to 8.1 percentage points per year since. About four-fifths of the increase in the prevalence of pages with fully AI-generated or AI-edited text comes from those belonging to domains on the periphery of the web graph that are not highly connected to other well-connected domains, while pages belonging to the most central domains on the web are least likely to contain fully AI-generated or AI-edited text. Further, generative AI has spread faster among English-language pages and .com domains, though we see rises across languages and domain categories, even after accounting for compositional effects. These results have implications specific to each role the public web plays. First, the growth in AI-influenced text means that generative AI has an increasing role in setting the conventions for how information is presented to the public, and how companies or governments communicate with their citizens. Second, because the crawlable web is a main input for training future language models, the rise of AI-generated or edited content means that earlier language models increasingly shape the conventions, style, and norms of newer ones.

For the purpose of this paper, we operationalize “AI-generated text” as text generated with or revised by language models. To identify AI-generated text, we take a holistic approach that views AI detection as a measurement error problem. We use multiple AI detectors and treat their output as imperfect indicators of text’s true origin (Bollen, 1989; Jacobs and Wallach, 2021). Commercial and open-source detectors infer AI involvement by identifying textual patterns correlated with language models’ writing styles. AI signatures vary across contexts and also appear in human writing, so we expect that the degree of measurement error will depend on the circumstances. In our evaluations, for example, the open Pangram model (Thai et al., 2026) has fewer false positives than Binoculars-Falcon (Hans et al., 2024) on .gov and .edu domains but more on .com domains (more detail in the Appendix section B). To address this context-specific measurment error, we build a Bayesian hierarchical model that combines detector outputs with labeled benchmarks and pre-2022 control crawls to estimate prevalence jointly with sensitivity and specificity. The early crawls inform false-positive rates under an assumption of low prevalence, while four benchmark datasets (one with texts from 9 languages) inform sensitivity and its variation across sources. We allow error rates to differ across contexts and to shift after the control period. The specificity adjustment is specific to each detector, language, centrality tier, top-level domain, and text length. The sensitivity adjustment varies across detector and language. Uncertainty about those rates enters the intervals for prevalence and its changes over time, allowing us to assess whether differences between groups and changes in their growth rates persist after accounting for detector error. Several previous studies also account for these errors, but in more limited contexts than we consider (Brooks et al., 2024; Russo et al., 2025; Liang et al., 2024; Russell et al., 2026; Elazar and Antoniak, 2026). We discuss related work further in Appendix A.

Our fundamental goals are to (i) estimate trends over time in the fraction of public-facing webpages using AI-generated text and, (ii) to determine how the prevalence varies across domain centrality, language, and top-level domain. Related to our first goal of understanding trends in prevalence over time, studies of newly archived English-language pages document a substantial increase in detected AI use between 2022 and mid-2025 (Dolezal et al., 2026). Graphite likewise finds a sharp initial increase among newly published English-language articles, followed by an approximately stable share over the five quarters from early 2025 through early 2026 (Graphite, 2025; Graphite, 2026). These studies discuss new content, however, rather than the total prevalence, which is our focus and is critical to understand how AI-generated text impacts users’ experiences and the composition of the web overall. Several other authors look at AI-generated text, but in specific contexts rather than the public facing web. Russell et al. (2026), for example, audit 186,000 articles from 1,500 American newspapers published in summer 2025 and find that roughly 9% carry detected AI use, concentrated mostly in small local outlets. The Pew Research Center does address the overall prevalence of AI-generated text, but restricts their analysis to English-language pages and report only the share of pages flagged by a particular AI-detector (Pew Research Center, 2026). As described above, individual AI detectors have context-specific false positive and false negative rates, meaning that a study reporting only the share of pages flagged as AI by a detector will inherit those biases. Pew also draws repeated random samples of English-language pages from Common Crawl (Pew Research Center, 2026), which means that the sampling distribution approximately mirrors that of the population, leaving relatively few examples of webpages in small groups (such as the ones mostly highly connected to other domains), unlike our design which is stratified to ensure we seen enough pages with rare characteristics to make meaningful between-group comparisons. papers.title: CASEL: Consequence-Aware Selective Execution for Reliable Long-Horizon Tool-Using Agents
papers.abstract: Tool-using language agents increasingly modify external systems, yet most runtime safeguards allocate scrutiny by generic uncertainty scores or coarse mutation heuristics. We introduce CASEL (Consequence-Aware Selective Execution Layer), a model-agnostic runtime allocation policy that combines calibrated failure probability, state-dependent consequence, reversibility, ambiguity, and evidence freshness to choose, for each proposed tool call, among direct execution, verification, sandboxing, clarification, approval, and abstention by minimizing a per-mode cost. We formalize direct execution as selective prediction and state and test the validity conditions of a finite-sample threshold and a trajectory risk ledger. In a controlled simulation over 20 seeds with 120,000 test actions each, in which every method has the same intervention menu and the same compute cost, CASEL reduces harmful-side-effect trajectories from 14.75 percent for an uncertainty-ranked gate to 7.02 percent and mean normalized harm from 0.184 to 0.123. A gate ranked by the product of failure probability and consequence reaches similar harm (5.82 percent, 0.120) but sends 45 percent more actions to human approval, and removing reversibility-aware routing raises the rate to 15.53 percent. A trajectory-level risk budget, in contrast, increases harm at equal cost (11.82 percent). Intervention effectiveness is assumed, not measured: the results rank allocation rules under the simulator's assumptions and do not establish deployment effectiveness.

papers.title: ADTGuard: Adaptive Depth-Time Safeguard for Streaming Inference in Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) can generate fluent responses to diverse user requests, yet streaming may expose users to harmful content before generation is complete. Existing guardrails face two limitations in this setting. First, post-hoc moderation at response or chunk boundaries delays intervention, risking harmful exposure when content is released before verification. Second, even with token-level detection, coarse response-level supervision does not specify when harmful content begins, while fixed-layer readouts may miss relevant safety signals at other depths. To address these limitations, we introduce ADTGuard, which checks each token before release, progressively refines token-level training targets, and adapts layer selection to the current prefix. ADTGuard models risk across depth and time through Depth-Time Safety Dynamics (DTSD), which integrates safety evidence across layers at each token and uses it to guide risk accumulation over successive tokens. To adapt the choice of observation layers to the current prefix, we propose the Causal Depth Router (CDR). With only response-level labels available, we further develop Risk-Onset Target Refinement (RTR) to progressively construct token-level training targets for both components. Through extensive experiments across multiple safety benchmarks, we demonstrate that ADTGuard consistently achieves strong streaming detection performance, matching or surpassing state-of-the-art safeguards while requiring only 16M trainable parameters and maintaining competitive per-token latency.

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in interactive settings where outputs are generated and delivered incrementally. Despite substantial progress in alignment and content moderation, capable models can still be induced to generate harmful or policy-violating content under adversarial or challenging inputs (Andriushchenko et al., 2025; Sharma et al., 2025). This is particularly consequential for autoregressive generation, where unsafe text may reach the user before a response-level safeguard can evaluate the completed response (Inan et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2025; Yu et al., 2026). Effective streaming safeguards must therefore assess risk as generation unfolds and enable intervention before harmful content is exposed to the user.

Obtaining such fine-grained token-level annotations manually is costly and difficult to scale. Broadcasting a harmful response label to every decoding position incorrectly marks early benign prefixes as unsafe (Cunningham et al., 2026; He et al., 2026), whereas manually designed temporal priors impose a shared risk progression across responses whose harmful content may emerge at different positions (Li et al., 2025b). papers.title: Natural Hard-Negative Mining from Positives for Instruction-Following Retrieval
papers.abstract: Instruction-following information retrieval (IFIR) requires retrievers to rank documents by both a query and its instance-specific instructions, yet instruction-conditioned contrastive supervision remains scarce. Existing synthetic methods typically fix a positive passage and generate additional negatives, overlooking the hard-negative potential of the original positive. We propose Natural Hard-Negative Mining (NHNM), which promotes convertible negatives under query-compatible instructions and repurposes original positives as natural instruction hard negatives. Its automated Candidate Cleaning, Reversal Construction, and Geometry Filtering pipeline produces compact, high-contrast supervision aligned with the pretrained retrieval space. Applied to MSMARCO, NHNM yields NHNM-MARCO, an IFIR training set of nearly 7K instances. On InstructIR and FollowIR, models with 568M to 4B parameters fine-tuned on NHNM-MARCO achieve strong instruction-following performance and match or surpass substantially larger retrievers in several settings. Controlled analyses and ablations attribute these gains to natural hard-negative supervision rather than model scale or training-data volume.

Instruction-following information retrieval (IFIR) requires retrievers to satisfy both a query and user instructions about aspects, scope, evidence, or exclusions. Instruction-aware supervision is therefore needed Weller et al. (2025a), but contrastive pairs whose relevance changes with the instruction are scarce and costly to annotate. Simply adding instructions to conventional tuples with fixed relevance labels lets models ignore them; effective supervision must expose instruction-conditioned relevance changes.

papers.title: Guided-RLVR: Guided Exploration in Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has shown strong empirical gains in improving the reasoning ability of large language models (LLMs) on tasks such as mathematics and programming. However, recent studies have shown that RLVR rollouts often collapse onto a narrow set of reasoning trajectories, limiting the explored reasoning space. Motivated by findings that thinking tokens at critical steps serve as critical structural elements in LLM reasoning pathways, we propose Guided-RLVR, a novel approach that augments RLVR with a lightweight controller. The controller strategically injects semantically meaningful steering tokens into the sampling distribution, encouraging the model to approach problems from multiple reasoning perspectives and thereby expanding the exploration space. Experiments on mathematical reasoning and code generation benchmarks show that Guided-RLVR consistently outperforms existing RLVR methods while producing more diverse reasoning trajectories.

Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities on reasoning-intensive tasks (Achiam et al. 2023; Team et al. 2024), from mathematical problem solving (Lightman et al. 2023) and code generation (Wei et al. 2023) to multi-step logical inference (Yao et al. 2023). While supervised fine-tuning establishes a strong foundation, reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has emerged as a powerful paradigm for pushing reasoning accuracy further, particularly in domains where correctness verification is available (Shao et al. 2024; Yu et al. 2026).

While supervised fine-tuning establishes a strong foundation, reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has emerged as a powerful paradigm for pushing reasoning accuracy further, particularly in domains where correctness verification is available (Shao et al. 2024; Yu et al. 2026).

Despite these successes, recent work has revealed a fundamental limitation: RLVR predominantly reinforces reasoning paths that already exist in the base model’s prior distribution (Tomihari and Sato 2026; Yue et al. 2025; Wu et al. 2025). While this reweighting improves pass@1 accuracy by increasing the probability of correct trajectories, it often fails to expand the set of problems the model can solve under repeated sampling. Instead, RLVR-trained models can exhibit distributional collapse, in which their rollouts concentrate on a narrow set of high-probability solution patterns and leave large regions of the reasoning space unexplored. This limits the value of inference-time sampling: even with a generous sampling budget, the model may repeatedly generate variations of the same approach rather than discover alternative strategies.

We examine this phenomenon by sampling 32 responses per problem on 200 MATH instances (Hendrycks et al. 2021) under vanilla RLVR and guided steering. Total variance is computed before dimensionality reduction as the trace of the covariance matrix of the standardized final-layer representations, equivalently the sum of variance across hidden dimensions; t-SNE (van der Maaten and Hinton 2008) is used only for visualization. As shown in Figure 1, vanilla RLVR produces a compact cluster, whereas guided steering spreads the rollout representations over a substantially broader region and increases total variance by nearly fourfold. This contrast indicates that steering-token interventions reduce the representational concentration observed under vanilla sampling. We observe the same trend with both GRPO (Shao et al. 2024) and DAPO (Yu et al. 2026) across mathematical reasoning benchmarks.

These observations motivate a more direct approach to expanding the exploration space. In reasoning tasks, certain thinking tokens, such as discourse connectives (“Therefore”, “However”) and reflective markers (“Wait”, “Since”), carry disproportionately high mutual information with respect to the final answer (Qian et al. 2026). These tokens appear at structural turning points in reasoning chains, where the model shifts between inductive generalization and deductive inference (Sloman and Sloman 2009; Cai et al. 2025). Rather than relying solely on stochastic temperature sampling, exploration can therefore be guided by promoting such tokens at selected points during generation.

Building on this insight, we introduce Guided-RLVR, which augments RLVR with a lightweight learned Logic Controller. During rollout generation, the controller is activated at high-entropy sentence boundaries and conditions on the policy’s hidden state to select a semantically meaningful steering token. It then boosts the selected token’s logit before sampling from the perturbed next-token distribution. The controller and policy are optimized jointly using the same group-relative advantages, reinforcing interventions associated with higher-reward rollouts. Consequently, the guided rollout distribution increases the likelihood of sampling low-prior, high-reward reasoning trajectories that vanilla RLVR rarely explores.

Complementary analyses of trajectory diversity and pass@kk scaling show that these gains are accompanied by more diverse reasoning trajectories and broader problem coverage under repeated sampling, supporting the intended role of Guided-RLVR in guided exploration.

papers.title: Does Your Generalist Skill Optimizer Really Incentivize Agentic Tasks? Rethinking Skill Optimization via Bipartite Attribution
papers.abstract: Skill optimizers adapt an agent to long-horizon tasks, such as repairing a terminal environment, by rewriting its skill, a natural-language procedure in its context, and keeping the edits that raise success on a small dev set. On such tasks success is noisy, so a gain on a small dev set does not show that an edit helps, and a success score does not show what the edit costs. We introduce BiPA, which replays an optimizer's acceptance rule on candidates identical to its seed to measure what selection alone reports, and records each episode as a bipartite graph of turns and the text they read to trace extra input tokens to the behavior behind them. Across three optimizers, three agentic benchmarks and two models, the learned skills succeed about as often as their hand-written seed, 0.1 points higher on average. Their dev gains vanish on test: keeping the best of several candidates on at most 30 tasks reports gains this large even when none changed. They read about 16% more input tokens: the optimizers almost always add rules, half to re-check work and some to act one call at a time, and the agent follows them as extra turns, each re-sending the whole conversation. Four principles follow: accept an edit only if its gain exceeds what selection alone reports; charge it for the turns it adds, not for its length; let the editor delete and merge rules; show it what earlier rules cost. Code is available at https://github.com/valleysprings/BiPA.git.

papers.intro:
A harness, such as OpenCode or SWE-agent, is the agentic scaffold that runs a language model as an agent: it gives the model its prompt and tools and runs its loop until the task is done (OpenCode contributors, 2025; Yang et al., 2024b). Built for software engineering, these harnesses now run agents on other long-horizon tasks, such as repairing a terminal environment, serving a customer or running a business workflow. An agent is adapted to a family of such tasks with a skill, a natural-language procedure that the harness places in the model’s context at the start of every task. Skill optimizers automate this, starting from a seed skill (Agrawal et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026): an editor model reads the trajectories, the logs of the agent’s runs on training tasks, and turns their successes and failures into rules, and a gate keeps an edit if the agent with the edited skill solves more tasks of a small development set, the dev set. These optimizers report gains, mostly on short, cheap tasks such as question answering, and controlled studies find the gains sparse and fragile (Liu et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026).

Long-horizon tasks expose three gaps. First, selection is noisy. Long tasks keep dev sets small and success is stochastic, so one run can rank two skills either way (Miller, 2024; Kapoor et al., 2025), and keeping the best of several comparisons reports a gain even when nothing changed, a winner’s curse (Smith and Winkler, 2006): a reported gain does not show that a skill helps. Second, success hides cost. Each turn, one request to the model, re-sends the whole history, so extra turns raise the input tokens read over a task, and a success score does not show them. Third, rules go uncredited. The editor writes several rules per edit and the gate scores the whole edit with one number, so no rule is tested alone and it stays unknown which rules change the agent.

For the first gap, it replays the optimizer’s acceptance rule on candidates identical to the seed, so any gain the rule reports comes from selection alone (Section 4.1). For the second, it records each attempt at a task as a bipartite graph between the agent’s turns and the text each turn reads (Section 4.2) and splits a rise in input tokens into more tool calls, the same calls over more turns, more text per turn and longer skill text (Sections 4.3 and 4.4). For the third, we sort each added rule into one of eight categories by what it asks the agent to do and compare the categories with the behavior the graph records (Section 5.3).
